CP1 Histology Key 150
Cardio Pulm 1 · Mon Oct 19 2026 · Histology I

Histology: the 150 key questions

150 questions, one per key fact, picked by working through every practice question on the full question page (learning questions left out; the partly-CP1 "Borderline" questions counted at low weight) and both 2026 CP1 histology TA reviews (Harlem and Great Falls), and keeping the facts that answer the most of them, either directly or by crossing out the impossible choices. Histology is mostly recognition, so the key facts carry what each structure looks like and how to tell it from its look-alikes. After you answer, the Key fact box states the whole fact, What it unlocks shows how the fact is usually tested, what it lets you eliminate and links to the straight-recall questions it answers, and Slides shows where the lectures and labs teach it. Questions it helps you answer, at the bottom, holds the full practice and TA questions you might not expect it to answer (vignettes and micrographs that never name it, answers reached by elimination, traps, questions asked from the other direction), answerable in place, each with how it follows from the main question.

Heart wall layers and pericardium

1unlocks 3TA ×11 not obvious
A shard of glass enters the anterior chest and passes into the right ventricular cavity. In what order does it cross the coverings and wall of the heart?
  1. A. Epicardium → fibrous pericardium → parietal pericardium → myocardium → endocardium
  2. B. Fibrous pericardium → parietal pericardium → epicardium → endocardium → myocardium
  3. C. Fibrous pericardium → visceral serous pericardium → parietal serous pericardium → myocardium → endocardium
  4. D. Parietal serous pericardium → fibrous pericardium → epicardium → endocardium → myocardium
  5. E. Fibrous pericardium → parietal serous pericardium → pericardial cavity → epicardium (visceral pericardium) → myocardium → endocardium
AnswerE. Fibrous pericardium → parietal serous pericardium → pericardial cavity → epicardium (visceral pericardium) → myocardium → endocardium
WhyThe fibrous pericardium is outermost; its inner face is lined by the parietal serous layer, then comes the pericardial cavity, then the visceral serous layer (= epicardium) on the heart, then myocardium and last the endocardium facing the lumen. Any sequence that puts visceral before parietal, or endocardium before myocardium, is wrong.
Key factOutside → inside: fibrous pericardium (tough, anchors the heart) → parietal serous pericardium (mesothelium lining the fibrous sac) → pericardial cavity (thin film of serous fluid) → visceral serous pericardium = epicardium (mesothelium) → subepicardial loose CT and fat (coronary vessels) → myocardium → endocardium (faces the chamber lumen).
Lumen outward (heart wall only): endocardium → myocardium → epicardium.
q90: the printed source key put adipose tissue most superficial (1) and fibrous pericardium 2. The page key note and the lecture (F0718:22: epicardium = mesothelium over loose CT with fat) put the epicardial fat deep to the serous pericardium: fibrous → serous → adipose → myocardium → endocardium. Follow the key note.
What it unlocks: 4 questions

The 1 question you might not expect it to answer is in the dropdown at the bottom.

How it shows up

  • Ordering drag-and-drop: inner → outer (endocardium, myocardium, visceral pericardium/epicardium, parietal pericardium); TA version from the chamber lumen toward the pericardial cavity
  • Penetrating-trauma vignette: order the knife or glass passes from the fibrous pericardium to the endocardium
  • Superficial → deep ordering that adds "adipose tissue": epicardial fat sits under the serous (visceral) mesothelium and above the myocardium

What it lets you eliminate

  • Visceral pericardium and epicardium are the same layer: never parietal after visceral going inward
  • Endocardium is always the last (innermost) layer; myocardium is always in the middle

Straight-recall questions it answers (3)

  • TAH14 Starting from the chamber lumen and moving outward toward the pericardial cavity, place in order: epicardium, endocardium, myocardium. → Endocardium → myocardium → epicardium

Questions it helps you answer (1)
Practice Q90Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
Order the layers of the heart from superficial to deep:
  1. Fibrous pericardium
  2. Serous pericardium
  3. Endocardium
  4. Adipose tissue
  5. Myocardium
AnswerFibrous pericardium 2; Serous pericardium 3; Endocardium 5; Adipose tissue 1; Myocardium 4
Key check: Key order (superficial→deep): Adipose tissue 1, Fibrous pericardium 2, Serous pericardium 3, Myocardium 4, Endocardium 5. 'Adipose tissue' as most superficial fits only the mediastinal/pericardial fat outside the fibrous pericardium (as drawn on the TA's slide-22 figure). Epicardial (subepicardial) fat, which carries the coronary vessels, lies deep to the visceral serous pericardium, i.e. between serous pericardium and myocardium (Fibrous → Serous → Adipose → Myocardium → Endocardium). — Confirmed on re-check; correct answer: Fibrous pericardium (1) -> Serous pericardium (2) -> Adipose tissue (3) -> Myocardium (4) -> Endocardium (5)
Key check: The key puts adipose tissue outermost, but the epicardial fat carrying the coronary vessels lies deep to the visceral serous pericardium, just above the myocardium. Answer used: Fibrous pericardium 1; Serous pericardium 2; Adipose tissue 3; Myocardium 4; Endocardium 5
WhyFrom outside in lie the fibrous pericardium, the serous pericardium (parietal layer, cavity, visceral mesothelium), subepicardial adipose tissue, myocardium, then endocardium lining the chambers.
How it follows from the main questionThe fat that belongs to the heart wall is epicardial: under the serous (visceral) mesothelium, above muscle → fibrous → serous → adipose → myocardium → endocardium. Putting adipose first (outermost) is the trap.

2unlocks 4
Fluid that accumulates in the pericardial cavity lies directly between which two layers?
  1. A. Myocardium and endocardium
  2. B. Parietal serous pericardium and visceral serous pericardium (epicardium)
  3. C. Fibrous pericardium and parietal pleura
  4. D. Epicardium and myocardium
  5. E. Fibrous pericardium and parietal serous pericardium
AnswerB. Parietal serous pericardium and visceral serous pericardium (epicardium)
WhyThe pericardial cavity is the space between the parietal serous layer (lining the fibrous sac) and the visceral serous layer, which is the mesothelial surface of the epicardium. The fibrous pericardium lies outside the parietal layer, so fluid or blood in the cavity never touches it.
Key factPericardial cavity = space between the parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium; holds a thin film of lubricating fluid (made by the mesothelium) that reduces friction.
  • Heart side = visceral serous pericardium = epicardium → blood or fluid in the cavity is in direct contact with the epicardium
  • Outer side = parietal serous layer lining the fibrous pericardium (the fibrous layer itself does not touch the fluid)
  • Myocardium and endocardium never face the cavity; the pleura belongs to the lungs
What it unlocks: 4 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Autopsy follow-up: "400 mL of blood in the pericardial cavity is in direct contact with..." → epicardium (distractors endocardium, fibrous pericardium, myocardium, parietal pleura)
  • "The pericardial space is lined by which layers?" → visceral and parietal pericardium
  • Short recall: "Blood in the pericardial cavity would be in contact with which of the following?"

What it lets you eliminate

  • Fibrous pericardium: outside the parietal serous layer, so not in contact
  • Parietal pleura / visceral pleura: lung coverings, wrong cavity
  • Endocardium, myocardium: deep to the epicardium

3unlocks 41 not obvious
Two pericardial disorders both restrict ventricular filling. Which statement is correct?
  1. A. Rupture of an infarct drains blood into the pleural cavity, causing tamponade
  2. B. Constrictive pericarditis is primarily a disease of the endocardium
  3. C. Constrictive pericarditis results from thinning of the fibrous pericardium
  4. D. In cardiac tamponade, blood or fluid in the pericardial cavity compresses the heart
  5. E. In cardiac tamponade, blood collects between the endocardium and the myocardium
AnswerD. In cardiac tamponade, blood or fluid in the pericardial cavity compresses the heart
WhyTamponade = blood/fluid in the pericardial cavity (e.g., hemopericardium from a ruptured infarct) that the inelastic fibrous pericardium cannot accommodate, so the heart is compressed and cannot fill. Constrictive pericarditis is a disease of the pericardium, which becomes thick, fibrotic and calcified, not thin.
Key factCardiac tamponade: blood or fluid builds up in the pericardial cavity (e.g., hemopericardium when a softened infarct ruptures, usually within ~3 weeks of an MI) → rigid fibrous pericardium cannot stretch → heart compressed → ↓ ventricular filling → hypotension, tachycardia, shock (pulsus paradoxus).
Constrictive pericarditis: inflammation of the pericardium (e.g., spread of tuberculosis) heals with thickening, fibrosis and calcification that obliterates the cavity and encases the heart → restricted filling → right-sided failure signs (hepatomegaly, ascites, leg edema) and a friction rub.
The Lippincott explanation for q1/q32 says blood fills the "peritoneal cavity (hemopericardium)"; that is a typo for the pericardial cavity.
What it unlocks: 4 questions

The 1 question you might not expect it to answer is in the dropdown at the bottom.

How it shows up

  • Classic vignette (repeated 3 times): 2 weeks after a massive MI, BP 80/40, pulse 100, death; autopsy shows a left ventricular rupture → cause of death = cardiac tamponade (distractors dissecting aortic aneurysm, pulmonary edema, pulmonary thromboembolism, septic shock)
  • TB patient with friction rub, ascites, hepatomegaly, edema → constrictive pericarditis → structure most affected = pericardium (distractors conducting system, coronary arteries, endocardium, myocardium)

What it lets you eliminate

  • A ruptured ventricle bleeds into the pericardial sac: not an aortic dissection, not a pulmonary embolus
  • Constrictive pericarditis: the pericardium, not endocardium, myocardium or conduction system

Questions it helps you answer (1)
Practice Q1Vignette never names it
Two weeks after suffering a massive heart attack, a 54-year-old man presents to the emergency room complaining of sharp pain on the left side of his chest. On physical examination, the patient is apprehensive and sweating. His blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg, and the pulse rate is 100 per minute. The patient expires shortly after admission. At autopsy, the left ventricle shows a rupture in the myocardial wall. What was the most likely cause of the patient’s death?
  1. (A) Cardiac tamponade
  2. (B) Dissecting aortic aneurysm
  3. (C) Pulmonary edema
  4. (D) Pulmonary thromboembolism
  5. (E) Septic shock
AnswerA. Cardiac tamponade
WhyRupture of a softened infarct floods the pericardial cavity with blood (hemopericardium), compressing the heart and blocking ventricular filling, which is cardiac tamponade.
Explanation from the source
Rupture of a myocardial infarct causes blood to fill the peritoneal cavity (hemopericardium). This medical catastrophe restricts the motion of the heart and is referred to as cardiac tamponade. When it happens, it typically occurs within the first 3 weeks following myocardial infarction. Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mm Hg drop in arterial blood pressure with inspiration) is commonly observed in patients with hemopericardium. Although aortic dissections (choice B) can break through to the pericardium, they do not rupture the heart wall. None of the other cardiovascular diseases are associated with rupture of the heart wall and cardiac tamponade. Keywords: Hemopericardium, cardiac tamponade
How it follows from the main questionRuptured ventricle bleeds into the pericardial cavity (hemopericardium) → the stiff sac compresses the heart → no filling, hypotension, tachycardia = cardiac tamponade. Not aortic dissection, pulmonary edema, embolism or sepsis. Also asked as Q32, Q89.

4unlocks 10TA ×3
A low-power H&E section through the atrioventricular junction shows (1) a pale outer zone of adipose tissue holding the coronary sinus and a branch of the circumflex artery, (2) a thick, dense, dark-pink mass of interlacing muscle, and (3) a thin lining facing the ventricular lumen from which the mitral valve projects. Zone (1) is the:
  1. A. Epicardium
  2. B. Myocardium
  3. C. Fibrous skeleton
  4. D. Subendocardium
  5. E. Endocardium
AnswerA. Epicardium
WhyThe pale, fat-rich outer zone carrying the coronary vessels is the epicardium; the thick dark muscle mass is the myocardium, and the thin luminal lining that gives rise to the valve is the endocardium. The fibrous skeleton is dense CT at the valve base, not an outer fatty layer.
Key factLow-power heart wall, lumen outward:
  • Endocardium = thin pale lining on the chamber (lumen) side; the valves are folds of it
  • Myocardium = thickest layer, dense dark-pink interlacing cardiac muscle (much thicker in ventricles)
  • Epicardium = pale outer layer of loose CT and fat holding the coronary arteries, coronary sinus and veins, covered by mesothelium
2026 lab right-ventricle section: arrow at the pale outer surface = epicardium; asterisk in the thick muscle = myocardium; arrowhead at the luminal surface = endocardium.
q2: one older review keyed "Endo, Myo and Pericardium"; the heart-wall layer is the epicardium (visceral pericardium), as in Dr Bruno's key.
What it unlocks: 13 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • "Identify the 3 layers of the heart" on a gross slice or low-power section (free response, labels A/B/C in any order)
  • "Which annotation indicates the epicardium? arrowhead / asterisk / arrow" (2026 lab and TA)
  • "Identify what the blue label is covering" (myocardium) and Lippincott autopsy "Identify the indicated layer" (thick middle layer = myocardium)
  • TA: "Identify A and C", then "Identify A, B and C again" on the AV-junction section; "What layer do the heart valves belong to?" → endocardium

What it lets you eliminate

  • A zone with fat or large vessels is never endocardium or subendocardium
  • The bulk of the wall is always myocardium
  • The surface facing the chamber, where valves attach, is endocardium

  • TAG31 Identify A, B and C again (same low-power heart section). → A = endocardium; B = myocardium; C = epicardium
  • TAG32 What is the Arrow indicating? → B. Epicardium

Epicardium

5unlocks 1TA ×2
A layer of the heart wall is also called the visceral pericardium. Which feature is found in this layer but NOT in the endocardium?
  1. A. A simple squamous surface layer
  2. B. Purkinje fibers in its deepest part
  3. C. Mesothelium over loose connective tissue with adipose tissue, coronary vessels and autonomic nerves
  4. D. Scattered smooth muscle cells beneath an endothelium
  5. E. Intercalated discs
AnswerC. Mesothelium over loose connective tissue with adipose tissue, coronary vessels and autonomic nerves
WhyThe epicardium (visceral pericardium) is mesothelium on loose CT with fat, coronary vessels and nerves. Both layers have a simple squamous surface, so A does not discriminate; Purkinje fibers and subendothelial smooth muscle belong to the endocardium; intercalated discs belong to the myocardium.
Key factEpicardium (outer layer) = visceral layer of serous pericardium:
  • surface simple squamous mesothelium (secretes lubricating pericardial fluid)
  • underlying loose CT with variable adipose tissue, the coronary arteries and veins, and autonomic nerves
Compare: endocardium = endothelium + CT with smooth muscle + subendocardium (Purkinje fibers); myocardium = cardiac muscle with gap junctions/intercalated discs; heart valve = fold of endocardium with a dense CT core; cardiac skeleton = dense irregular CT.
What it unlocks: 3 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • TA: "outermost layer of the heart wall: tissue composition?" → simple squamous mesothelium over loose CT with fat, vessels, nerves (distractors endothelium + conducting fibers, smooth muscle/elastic layers, DICT, spiral cardiac muscle)
  • "Which layer of the heart is lined by mesothelium?" → visceral pericardium (epicardium)
  • TA matching: mesothelium + loose CT + nerves + fat → epicardium; gap junctions → myocardium; endothelium + subendocardial conducting fibers → endocardium; fold with dense CT core → valve

What it lets you eliminate

  • Endothelium + conducting fibers → endocardium; smooth muscle + elastic layers → vessel media; DICT → cardiac skeleton; spiral cardiac muscle → myocardium
  • Fibrous pericardium and Purkinje fibers are not lined by mesothelium

Used together with

Myocardium (cardiac muscle) on H&E; Endocardium: three sublayers; Valve histology: endocardial fold, avascular dense CT

6unlocks 12TA ×2
A section of atrial wall shows, from the free surface inward: a single row of flattened cells, a zone of loose connective tissue containing an oval bundle of wavy fibers and a few adipocytes, then cross-cut striated muscle bundles. The surface cells plus the loose connective tissue zone are the:
  1. A. Endocardium
  2. B. Subendocardium
  3. C. Visceral pleura
  4. D. Epicardium
  5. E. Fibrous pericardium
AnswerD. Epicardium
WhyFlat mesothelium over loose CT with a nerve and fat, resting directly on myocardium, is the epicardium. The endocardium faces a chamber with no fat or nerves beneath it; the fibrous pericardium is dense CT not attached to the muscle; pleura covers the lung.
Key factEpicardium micrograph (lab labels Mes / CT / N / F / Ep / M):
  • Mes = thin wavy row of flat mesothelial cells on the free surface (faces the pericardial cavity)
  • CT = pale loose connective tissue; N = autonomic nerve; F = fat (adipocytes = empty white rings; can be abundant, with large coronary vessels, M/A/F labels)
  • M = cardiac muscle (myocardium) directly below, with intercalated discs and gap junctions
Rule: fat, nerves or a big vessel under the surface layer → epicardium, not endocardium.
TAG35: the TA answer slide reads "Myocardium - B, Epicardium - A", but on the image A sits in the muscle bundles (M) and B in the connective tissue beside the Ep bracket, so A = myocardium and B = epicardium. Learn the layer by its features, not the TA letter key.

In epicardial connective tissue, a circled structure is a solid oval bundle of pale, wavy fibers with many elongated nuclei; it has no lumen and no red blood cells. Beside it is a vessel with a thick muscular wall around a small round lumen. The circled structure is a(n):
  1. A. Lymphatic vessel
  2. B. Arteriole
  3. C. Nerve
  4. D. Venule
  5. E. Cardiac muscle bundle
AnswerC. Nerve
WhyA solid bundle of wavy fibers with elongated (Schwann cell) nuclei and no lumen is an autonomic nerve. The arteriole is the thick-walled vessel beside it; venules and lymphatics both have a lumen, and cardiac muscle is striated and lies below in the myocardium.
Key factThe epicardium carries the heart's nerves and vessels:
  • Nerve = solid oval bundle, pale wavy fibers, elongated nuclei, no lumen, no RBCs (sympathetic, parasympathetic and visceral afferent fibers)
  • Arteriole / coronary artery branch = thick smooth-muscle wall, small round lumen
  • Venule / cardiac vein = thin wall, wider irregular lumen with RBCs
  • Cardiac muscle = striated fibers below, in the myocardium
What it unlocks: 3 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Lippincott myxoma vignette: "The epicardium ... identify the structure indicated by the circle" (arteriole, cardiac muscle, connective tissue, nerve, venule)
  • Lab "Blue?" arrow on the bundle labelled N → autonomic nerve
  • Labelling the epicardium image: B = nerve, D = fat

What it lets you eliminate

  • Anything with a lumen or red cells is a vessel, not a nerve
  • Thick wall + small round lumen = arteriole; thin wall + wide lumen = venule

During coronary artery bypass surgery, the main coronary arteries are found and grafted in which layer of the heart wall?
  1. A. Fibrous pericardium
  2. B. Epicardium
  3. C. Endocardium
  4. D. Endomysium
  5. E. Myocardium
AnswerB. Epicardium
WhyThe main coronary arteries and cardiac veins travel in the subepicardial fat of the epicardium; only smaller branches penetrate the myocardium. The endomysium carries capillaries, not the main vessels, and the fibrous pericardium is the outer sac, not the heart wall.
Key factLeft and right coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses (elastic recoil of the aorta drives blood into them between contractions) and run with the cardiac veins and nerves in the epicardium (subepicardial loose CT and fat); their branches then penetrate and supply the myocardium.
A thick-walled muscular vessel in epicardial fat = branch of a coronary artery (not a cardiac vein, the coronary sinus or the internal thoracic artery).
What it unlocks: 3 questions

The 1 question you might not expect it to answer is in the dropdown at the bottom.

How it shows up

  • Dr Bruno lecture quiz Q2: "Where are the main blood vessels which supply the heart located?" (epicardium, pericardium, myocardium, endocardium, endomysium)
  • "Which layer of the heart contains the coronary arteries?"
  • Lippincott myxoma vignette: "the structure within the circle represents a branch of which blood vessel?" → coronary artery

What it lets you eliminate

  • Endomysium: capillaries only; pericardium: the sac, not the wall
  • Cardiac vein / coronary sinus: thin-walled venous channels, not a muscular artery

Practice Q36Vignette never names it
A 56-year-old woman is diagnosed with a left atrial myxoma. The tumor is removed, and the surgical specimen is examined by light microscopy. The tumor margin shows normal heart tissue (shown in the image). The structure within the circle represents a branch of which of the following blood vessels?
  1. (A) Cardiac vein
  2. (B) Coronary artery
  3. (C) Coronary sinus
  4. (D) Internal thoracic artery
  5. (E) Supreme thoracic artery
Answer(B) Coronary artery
WhyThe thick-walled vessel with concentric smooth muscle in the heart wall is a branch of the coronary arteries, which arise from the aortic sinuses and supply the myocardium.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Coronary artery. The photomicrograph shows an arteriole and an accompanying venule embedded in adipose connective tissue. The heart receives arterial blood supply from the right and left coronary arteries— branches off the initial part of the ascending aorta. The coronary arteries give rise to numerous branches that travel within the adipose tissue of the epicardium near the surface of the heart. Cardiac veins (choice A) accompany branches of the coronary arteries. These veins drain to the coronary sinus (choice C) on the posterior wall of the heart, which, in turn, empties into the right atrium. None of the other blood vessels supply the heart. Keywords: Arteries, coronary arteries
How it follows from the main questionThick muscular wall, small round lumen = artery branch; arteries in epicardial fat are branches of the coronary arteries. Cardiac veins and the coronary sinus are thin-walled; thoracic arteries never enter the wall.
Slide (1)

Myocardium and intercalated discs

9unlocks 112 not obvious
A high-power H&E field shows branching striated fibers, each cell with one (occasionally two) large oval central nucleus surrounded by a pale zone, dark transverse step-like lines where cells meet end to end, and many capillaries between fibers. This field is:
  1. A. Subendocardium with Purkinje fibers
  2. B. Epicardium
  3. C. Skeletal muscle
  4. D. Smooth muscle of a vessel media
  5. E. Myocardium
AnswerE. Myocardium
WhyBranching striated fibers with 1–2 central nuclei, a perinuclear clear zone and intercalated discs = cardiac muscle = myocardium. Skeletal muscle has many peripheral nuclei and no discs; Purkinje fibers are much larger and paler; smooth muscle is not striated.
Key factCardiac muscle (myocardium) on LM:
  • branching, cross-striated fibers
  • one or two oval central nuclei with a pale perinuclear zone; golden-brown lipofuscin granules at the nuclear poles = residues of lysosomal digestion ("wear and tear" pigment)
  • intercalated discs = dark transverse, step-like lines at cell-to-cell junctions (not node of Ranvier, perimysium, endomysium or lipofuscin)
  • thin endomysium rich in capillaries (capillary = one endothelial cell around a lumen about one RBC wide, ± pericyte)
Myocardium = the muscular middle layer of the wall: thickest layer, concentric/spiral sheets, thicker in ventricles.
What it unlocks: 11 questions

The 2 questions you might not expect it to answer are in the dropdown at the bottom.

How it shows up

  • "Identify (this layer)" on a field of striated fibers: epicardium / endocardium / myocardium (sometimes with subendocardium and skeletal muscle as options)
  • 2026 lab: "Are central nuclei, branching myofibers and intercalated discs visible?" and "At higher magnification, what features are discernible?"; "Describe the nuclei of cardiac myocytes"
  • Arrow on a dark transverse line: node of Ranvier / perimysium / intercalated disc / endomysium / lipofuscin
  • "Which layer contains the muscular wall of the heart?"; capillaries between cross-cut fibers (capillary vs internal elastic lamina, endothelial cell, elastic artery)

What it lets you eliminate

  • Many peripheral nuclei → skeletal; no striations, cigar nuclei → smooth; large pale cells → Purkinje
  • Golden-brown perinuclear granules are lipofuscin, not intercalated discs

On a routine H&E section, which feature distinguishes cardiac muscle from skeletal muscle?
  1. A. Fibers made of separate cells joined end to end at intercalated discs
  2. B. A rich capillary network in the connective tissue

  4. D. Sarcomeres between adjacent Z lines

WhyA cardiac "fiber" is a chain of separate cells joined end to end at intercalated discs; a skeletal fiber is one long multinucleated cell. Striations, A/I bands, sarcomeres, actin and capillaries are shared by both, so they cannot discriminate.
Key factIntercalated discs uniquely identify cardiac muscle: fibers = many cells in series joined end to end (branched; 1–2 central nuclei).
Skeletal: one huge multinucleated cell, many peripheral nuclei, no discs.
Smooth: spindle cells, one central cigar-shaped nucleus, no striations, no discs.
Shared by cardiac and skeletal (never the answer): cross-striations, A and I bands, sarcomeres between Z lines, actin thin filaments, sarcolemma, capillary network. If asked what "uniquely identifies" cardiac muscle, answer intercalated discs.

WhyIntercalated discs hold fasciae adherentes (cadherin; anchor actin), desmosomes (desmoglein + desmocollin; anchor intermediate filaments) and gap junctions (connexons). Hemidesmosomes bind a cell to the basal lamina, not cell to cell, so they are absent.
Key factIntercalated disc = junctional complex of three junctions:
  • Fascia adherens: cadherins; anchors actin thin filaments of the end sarcomere
  • Desmosome (macula adherens): desmoglein + desmocollin; anchors intermediate filaments; holds cells together during contraction
  • Gap junction: connexons; electrical coupling
NOT present: hemidesmosomes (cell to basal lamina), zonula occludens (tight junction of epithelia), focal adhesions. (Zona fasciculata is adrenal cortex, not a junction.)

  • Longitudinal/lateral part (parallel to myofibrils): gap junctions (narrow, closely apposed membranes)
Skeletal muscle EM: regular sarcomeres with no stepwise cell-to-cell junction.

WhyGap junctions (connexons) are low-resistance ionic channels that pass depolarization from cell to cell, so the myocardium contracts as a coordinated functional syncytium. A = hemidesmosome, B = fascia adherens, C = SA node, D = desmosome.

Which statement about the large, pale subendocardial fibers of the ventricles is true?
  1. A. They set the heart rate because they fire faster than the SA node
  2. B. They are modified neurons related to the Purkinje cells of the cerebellum
  3. C. They are cardiomyocytes swollen by ischemia
  4. D. They are modified cardiac muscle cells that rapidly conduct the impulse to the ventricular myocardium
  5. E. They are the principal cells of the sinoatrial node
AnswerD. They are modified cardiac muscle cells that rapidly conduct the impulse to the ventricular myocardium
WhyPurkinje fibers are modified cardiac muscle cells of the conduction system that rapidly conduct the impulse from the bundle branches to the ventricular muscle. They share only a name with cerebellar Purkinje neurons, are not SA-node cells or ischemic swelling, and fire slower than the SA node.
Key factPurkinje fibers = modified cardiomyocytes specialized for conduction, not contraction (linked to each other and to contractile cells by desmosomes and gap junctions).
Bundle branches → subendocardial Purkinje network near the apex → rapid spread to all ventricular muscle → coordinated contraction from apex to base.
Damage → impaired ventricular conduction (not SA-node initiation, not valve support). Intrinsic rate slower than the SA node. Not neurons (≠ cerebellar Purkinje cells).

Conduction system

Which sequence correctly traces normal cardiac depolarization?
  1. A. Purkinje fibers → bundle branches → bundle of His → AV node → SA node
  2. B. AV node → SA node → atrial myocardium → bundle of His → Purkinje fibers → ventricular myocardium
  3. C. SA node → bundle of His → AV node → Purkinje fibers → atrial myocardium
  4. D. SA node → AV node → ventricular myocardium → Purkinje fibers
  5. E. SA node → atrial myocardium → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricular myocardium
AnswerE. SA node → atrial myocardium → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricular myocardium
WhyThe SA node fires first (fastest intrinsic rate = pacemaker), the impulse spreads through atrial muscle to the AV node (brief delay so the atria finish emptying), then the bundle of His, the right and left bundle branches, the Purkinje fibers, and finally the ventricular myocardium.
Key factSA node = pacemaker: earliest, fastest spontaneous depolarization (sympathetic fibers only modulate the rate; AV node, His and Purkinje are slower backups).
Sequence: SA node → atrial myocardium → AV node (delay) → AV bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricular myocardium.
All nodal and conducting cells are modified cardiac muscle cells.

  • Ordering 6 items: SA node, atrial myocardium, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fiber, ventricular myocardium

What it lets you eliminate

  • AV node, His bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers: conduct, but are not the pacemaker
  • Sympathetic fibers change the rate but do not generate the rhythm

AnswerC. Dense irregular connective tissue
WhyThe cardiac skeleton is dense irregular connective tissue: fibrous rings around the valves and the bases of the aorta and pulmonary trunk, the fibrous trigones and the membranous septum. It is not cartilage, tendon-like dense regular CT or loose CT.

  • surrounds and anchors the valves and extends into the valve cusps and chordae tendineae; gives insertion to atrial and ventricular muscle
On a valve-base section it lies in the endocardium between atrium and ventricle (blue in trichrome).

WhyThe dense CT of the cardiac skeleton does not conduct, so it electrically insulates atria from ventricles; the only electrical bridge is the AV bundle, which pierces the skeleton. The skeleton anchors valves and muscle but never initiates or conducts impulses.

Which feature belongs to the semilunar valves but not to the atrioventricular valves?
  1. A. Papillary muscles tense them during ventricular contraction
  2. B. They separate the atria from the ventricles
  3. C. They include the mitral valve
  4. D. Their cusps are tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles
  5. E. They have three cusps and no muscular support
AnswerE. They have three cusps and no muscular support
WhySemilunar valves (aortic, pulmonary) separate the ventricles from the circulation and have three cusps that brace each other like a tripod, with no muscular support. AV valves (tricuspid, mitral) separate atria from ventricles and are braced by chordae tendineae tensed by papillary muscles.
Key factAV valves: tricuspid (right) and bicuspid = mitral (left); separate atria from ventricles; folds of fibrous tissue; closed by blood pressure; papillary muscles tense chordae tendineae so the cusps do not evert.
Semilunar valves: pulmonary (RV → pulmonary trunk) and aortic (LV → aorta); separate ventricles from circulation; 3 cusps "like a tripod"; no muscular support.
2 AV + 2 SL valves. All valves close passively by pressure; muscles only brace the AV cusps.
q95 (key: semilunar valves) is loosely worded: no valve is closed by muscle contraction; all close passively by pressure (F0718:51 "blood pressure closes valve"). Its intended point is that only AV valves have muscular (papillary muscle and chordae) support.

28TA ×2
A chorda tendinea attached to the mitral valve ruptures. Which finding is expected?
  1. A. Aortic regurgitation into the left ventricle
  2. B. Mitral regurgitation: the unsupported leaflet lets blood flow back into the left atrium
  3. C. Mitral stenosis from rigid, calcified leaflets
  4. D. Cardiac tamponade
  5. E. Failure of the SA node to fire
AnswerB. Mitral regurgitation: the unsupported leaflet lets blood flow back into the left atrium
WhyChordae tendineae, tensed by papillary muscles, keep AV cusps from everting during ventricular contraction. Rupture → the mitral cusp flails → incomplete closure = regurgitation (insufficiency) → backflow into the left atrium. Stenosis is narrowing that stops the valve opening fully.
Key factRegurgitation = insufficiency: the valve does not close completely → blood leaks back into the preceding chamber (murmur). Stenosis: stiff, calcified, narrowed valve that does not open fully.
AV-valve support chain: papillary muscles → chordae tendineae → cusps. Rupture of chordae or a papillary muscle → cusp everts → mitral regurgitation into the left atrium.

Bacterial damage strips the endothelium from part of a valve cusp. What is the first intravascular event, and what is the clot that forms on the cusp called?
  1. A. Fibroblast proliferation; hematoma
  2. B. Platelet aggregation; embolus
  3. C. Cardiomyocyte proliferation; vegetation
  4. D. Platelet aggregation; thrombus
  5. E. Smooth muscle migration; atheroma
AnswerD. Platelet aggregation; thrombus
WhyIntact endothelium is an antithrombogenic barrier. When it is injured, platelets aggregate on the exposed surface and build a thrombus, a clot attached to the wall or endocardium. A thrombus fragment that breaks off and travels is an embolus; cardiomyocytes cannot proliferate.
Key factEndothelium (lining the endocardium and the valve cusps) normally maintains an antithrombogenic barrier. Injury → platelet aggregation → thrombus (clot attached to the vessel or endocardial wall); detached, travelling fragment = embolus; atheroma = intimal plaque of arteries; hematoma = blood in tissue.
Vegetations on valves (e.g., viridans streptococci entering the blood after dental surgery) = infective endocarditis → the infected layer is the endocardium (valves are folds of it), not epicardium or myocardium.

A coronary artery is occluded by thrombus on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. Which layer sustains the primary injury, and what happens to its cells?

Early histology: coagulative necrosis (hypereosinophilic fibers, loss of nuclei, contraction bands), then inflammation and repair by scar (no regeneration).

  4. D. Collagen of a healed scar
  5. E. Purkinje fibers

WhyMultiple dense transverse bands within one cardiomyocyte = contraction bands (hypercontracted sarcomeres) → myocardial infarction. Normal intercalated discs are thin step-like lines only at the ends of cells, one per cell junction.
Key factContraction bands: thick, dark eosinophilic transverse bands, many within a single cell, in hypereosinophilic fibers with lost nuclear detail → myocardial infarction (heart attack).
Intercalated discs: thin dark step-like lines at cell-to-cell junctions (end to end) → healthy cardiac muscle.

Months after a large myocardial infarction, what has replaced the dead muscle in the infarcted region?
  1. A. Dense collagenous scar tissue
  2. B. New cardiomyocytes produced by hyperplasia
  3. C. Normal myocardium after complete resolution
  4. D. Smooth muscle derived from fibroblasts
  5. E. Hyaline cartilage
AnswerA. Dense collagenous scar tissue
WhyAdult cardiomyocytes cannot divide, so an infarct heals through granulation tissue that matures into a dense collagenous (fibrous) scar (about a month after the event). The scar does not contract, so pump function falls and heart failure can follow.
Key factAdult cardiac muscle cells are permanent (no mitosis):
  • Infarct → coagulative necrosis → inflammation → granulation tissue → fibrous scar (dense collagen) by about 1 month; scar is non-contractile → ↓ contractility, heart failure
  • Chronic pressure overload (e.g., hypertension) → the heart enlarges by hypertrophy (bigger cells, more myofibrils), not hyperplasia

Arteries, veins and the vessel wall

Vessel wall: the three tunics

33unlocks 5TA ×73 not obvious
A micrograph of an artery wall has the lumen at the top. An arrow marks the thin strip right at the lumen: a single row of flattened nuclei resting on a small amount of connective tissue, just above a thick band of circular smooth muscle. Which layer is marked?
  1. A. Internal elastic lamina
  2. B. Tunica media
  3. C. Tunica intima
  4. D. Tunica adventitia
  5. E. Vasa vasorum
AnswerC. Tunica intima
WhyThe thin luminal layer of endothelium (simple squamous) on subendothelial connective tissue is the tunica intima. The internal elastic lamina is only its outer boundary line, the thick smooth-muscle band below it is the media, and the loose connective tissue with small vessels outside is the adventitia.
Key factThree tunics, from the lumen outward:
  • Intima = endothelium (simple squamous) + subendothelial connective tissue (a few SM cells in large arteries); in arteries it ends at the internal elastic lamina. Thin strip at the lumen.
  • Media = circular smooth muscle + elastic fibers/lamellae; the thick middle band of arteries. Nuclei in the media are smooth muscle cells.
  • Adventitia = loose (to dense irregular) collagenous connective tissue with fibroblasts, vasa vasorum and nerves; outermost, blends into the surroundings (in large veins it also holds longitudinal SM bundles).
To name a layer on a micrograph, find the lumen edge first (images are often upside down), then count outward.

How it shows up

  • TA micrographs of a vessel wall with an arrow or double arrow: "Identify the layer" (intima, media, adventitia) or "What are the two layers indicated?" (intima and media).
  • Vignette describing the innermost layer of simple squamous cells on a basement membrane and subendothelial tissue, with internal elastic lamina and vasa vasorum as distractors.
  • "Which correctly identifies the tissue composition of the three tunics?" with cuboidal or stratified epithelium as traps.
  • Autopsy aorta: "Identify layer A" (the middle layer) and "identify the cells whose nuclei are marked" in the media (smooth muscle cells).

What it lets you eliminate

  • Any option giving the intima a cuboidal or stratified epithelium: the lining is always simple squamous endothelium.
  • Internal elastic lamina is a boundary line and vasa vasorum are vessels inside the adventitia: neither is a tunic.
  • Fibroblasts, adipocytes, macrophages or cardiac muscle cells as the nuclei of the media: they are smooth muscle cells.

What is the wavy inner line, and what does finding both lines tell you?

  2. B. One of many elastic lamellae; the vessel is an elastic artery
  3. C. Basal lamina; the vessel is a capillary
  4. D. External elastic lamina; the vessel is a vein
  5. E. Internal elastic lamina; the vessel is an artery
AnswerE. Internal elastic lamina; the vessel is an artery
WhyThe internal elastic lamina is a fenestrated elastin sheet at the intima-media border (wavy because the artery contracts after death). An IEL plus an external elastic lamina at the media-adventitia border bracket the media of an artery. An elastic artery would show dozens of lamellae, not two lines.
Key factElastic laminae
  • Internal elastic lamina (IEL): wavy/scalloped line, dark on elastic stain and glassy pink on H&E, at the intima-media border; counted as part of the intima; most prominent in muscular arteries (the aorta has one too, as its first lamella).
  • External elastic lamina (EEL): thinner line at the media-adventitia border.
  • IEL + EEL = artery. Veins lack distinct laminae (at most a thin IEL in the largest veins).
q221 (and the TA table) say veins lack IEL/EEL; the lab manual (F0699:6) and q302's source mention a thin internal elastic membrane in large or larger medium veins. Distinct IEL + EEL around a thick muscular media still means artery.

In an elastic-stained aorta, the dark lamellar media is surrounded by a pale outer zone of loose connective tissue containing small arteries and veins that send branches into the outer media. What are these small vessels, and what do they do?
  1. A. Arteriovenous shunts; they bypass capillary beds for thermoregulation
  2. B. Vasa vasorum; they supply the outer wall, which is too thick to be fed from the lumen
  3. C. Pericytes; they stabilize the endothelium
  4. D. Nervi vasorum; they set the tone of the media
  5. E. Lymphatic vessels; they drain the vessel wall
AnswerB. Vasa vasorum; they supply the outer wall, which is too thick to be fed from the lumen
WhyVasa vasorum ("vessels of the vessels") run in the adventitia of large arteries and veins and feed the adventitia and outer media, which are too far from the lumen for diffusion; they do for the vessel wall what the coronary arteries do for the heart. Nerves are solid bundles with no lumen.
Key factVasa vasorum = small arteries, capillaries and veins in the tunica adventitia of large vessels (elastic arteries, large veins; muscular arteries may have them), branching into the outer media.
  • Function: oxygen and nutrients to the outer wall (the inner wall is fed from the lumen); analogous to the coronary arteries.
  • Recognition: small round vessels with lumens (often with RBCs) in the pale loose connective tissue outside the media; also in the adventitia of medium veins and the vena cava.
  • Not a layer, never in the intima; arterioles and capillaries have none.

Elastic arteries

37unlocks 16TA ×32 not obvious
A cross-section of a large vessel shows a thin intima, a very thick media made of dozens of concentric wavy elastic sheets alternating with smooth muscle cells, and a thinner outer coat containing small vessels. Which statement about this vessel is correct?
  1. A. It is a muscular artery; the dark bands are its internal and external elastic laminae
  2. B. It is a medium-sized vein, since its adventitia contains small vessels
  3. C. It is a large vein such as the vena cava; the bands are longitudinal smooth muscle
  4. D. It is a muscular artery such as the popliteal artery
  5. E. It is an elastic (conducting) artery such as the aorta or pulmonary trunk
AnswerE. It is an elastic (conducting) artery such as the aorta or pulmonary trunk
WhyDozens of concentric wavy elastic lamellae filling a very thick media define an elastic artery (aorta, pulmonary trunk and their large branches). A muscular artery such as the popliteal has only two laminae (IEL, EEL) around a smooth-muscle media, and a vena cava's thick layer is the adventitia with smooth-muscle bundles.
Key factElastic (conducting) artery = aorta, pulmonary trunk and arteries, large branches (brachiocephalic, common carotid, subclavian).
  • Intima: endothelium + connective tissue with some smooth muscle.
  • Media: very thick; many concentric, fenestrated, wavy elastic lamellae alternating with layers of smooth muscle (the SM cells are the media's only cells and make its elastin). H&E: stacked wavy pink sheets; elastic stain: the whole media is dark ("curly ramen").
  • Adventitia: relatively thin connective tissue with vasa vasorum and nerves.
vs muscular artery: one wavy IEL + EEL around a smooth-muscle media with little elastic.

Which pairing of vessel type and functional role is correct?
  1. A. Elastic artery: stretches in systole and recoils in diastole, keeping blood flowing between beats
  2. B. Arteriole: low-resistance conducting vessel
  3. C. Capillary: capacitance vessel holding most of the blood volume
  4. D. Muscular artery: primary site of vascular resistance
  5. E. Large vein: distributing vessel that directs blood to organs
AnswerA. Elastic artery: stretches in systole and recoils in diastole, keeping blood flowing between beats
WhyElastic (conducting) arteries store the energy of systole in their elastic lamellae and recoil in diastole, smoothing pulsatile output into continuous flow (and pushing blood into the coronaries between beats). Resistance belongs to arterioles, distribution to muscular arteries, exchange to capillaries, capacitance to veins.
Key factElastic fibers/lamellae (elastin on fibrillin microfibrils) let arteries stretch and recoil: the aorta expands in systole and recoils in diastole → continuous downstream flow and maintained diastolic pressure; elastic rebound drives coronary filling between contractions.
Functional ladder (for elimination):
  • Elastic artery = conducting, low resistance, recoil
  • Muscular artery = distributing (smooth muscle constricts/dilates)
  • Arteriole = resistance (primary site; blood pressure control)
  • Capillary = exchange; Vein = capacitance (most of the blood, low pressure)

What it lets you eliminate

Two vessels of similar outer diameter lie side by side. Vessel 1 has a large, flattened, irregular lumen and a thin wall whose outer collagen coat is thicker than its muscle layer. Vessel 2 has a smaller round lumen, a thick muscular wall and a scalloped inner line. Which statement is correct?
  1. A. 1 is a vein: its lumen diameter exceeds its wall thickness
  2. B. They can only be told apart by the presence of endothelium
  3. C. 2 is a lymphatic vessel, because its lumen is round
  4. D. 1 is an artery, because arteries have larger lumens
  5. E. 2 is a vein, because veins have more smooth muscle

WhyJudge the thickness of the media relative to the lumen. An artery has a thick muscular media around a round lumen with a wavy IEL; a vein has a thin wall, a wide, collapsed or irregular lumen (lumen diameter exceeds wall thickness) and an adventitia thicker than its media. Endothelium and connective tissue are in both, so they decide nothing.
Key factArtery vs vein of similar size (wall vs lumen):
  • Artery: round regular lumen, thick media relative to lumen, wavy IEL, media thicker than adventitia.
  • Vein: larger, irregular or flattened lumen (often holding blood), lumen diameter exceeds wall thickness, thin media, adventitia thicker than media, may show valves.
  • Endothelium, smooth muscle and connective tissue occur in both → useless as discriminators.

  1. A. 1 = large vein; 2 = elastic artery; 3 = lymph node
  2. B. 1 = lymphatic vessel; 2 = arteriole; 3 = nerve
  3. C. 1 = muscular artery; 2 = medium vein; 3 = skeletal muscle
  4. D. 1 = medium vein; 2 = muscular artery; 3 = peripheral nerve
  5. E. 1 = medium vein; 2 = elastic artery; 3 = peripheral nerve
AnswerD. 1 = medium vein; 2 = muscular artery; 3 = peripheral nerve
WhyA neurovascular bundle pairs a muscular (distributing) artery with its companion medium-sized vein and a peripheral nerve. The vein is the larger, thinner-walled, irregular lumen; the artery the smaller round one with a thick media and wavy IEL; the nerve is solid with no lumen. Elastic arteries and large veins sit near the heart, not in limb bundles.
Key factNeurovascular bundle (lab): muscular artery + medium-sized vein + peripheral nerve in one connective tissue sheath.
  • Artery: smaller, round, regular lumen; thick wall; IEL visible even on H&E.
  • Vein: larger, irregular lumen; wall-to-lumen ratio much smaller than the artery's.
  • Nerve: solid round bundle(s), no lumen.
So in any limb or neurovascular-bundle stem the artery is muscular (not elastic, not an arteriole) and the vein is medium (not large).

WhyVaricose veins are enlarged, tortuous superficial veins (saphenous veins and tributaries) with incompetent valves and/or a dilated wall, common with prolonged standing. Flow is turbulent and slow, the capillary bed is engorged and fluid leaks into the skin → stasis (venous) dermatitis and venous ulcers.
Key factVenous insufficiency and varicose veins (2026 lab):
  • Vessels: superficial leg veins (great/small saphenous and tributaries), not deep veins, arteries, lymphatics or nerves.
  • Cause: incompetent venous valves and/or dilation; more common with long periods of standing.
  • Physiology: turbulent, slow flow, engorged capillary bed, fluid leaks into the skin.
  • Complications: venous (stasis) dermatitis and venous ulcer (medial ankle, lower leg).

A 28-year-old woman collapses with sudden chest pain and dies the next day. Autopsy shows a large thromboembolus at the bifurcation of the right pulmonary artery. Where did it most likely form?
  1. A. Vegetations on the aortic valve
  2. B. A left ventricular mural thrombus
  3. C. Deep veins of the leg
  4. D. Superficial varicose veins of the leg
  5. E. A coronary atherosclerotic plaque
AnswerC. Deep veins of the leg
WhyMost pulmonary emboli come from deep vein thrombosis in the leg: the clot travels up the inferior vena cava, through the right heart, into the pulmonary arteries. Superficial varices may clot but rarely embolize, and left-heart or arterial sources embolize to systemic arteries, not the lungs.
Key factDVT vs varices
  • Varicose veins are superficial (saphenous); thrombi there rarely embolize, so varices are not a common cause of DVT.
  • DVT forms in the deep veins of the leg → embolus via IVC → right heart → pulmonary artery (pulmonary embolism).
  • Left-heart or arterial clots (mural thrombus, plaques, endocarditis) go to systemic arteries.

What it lets you eliminate

A tall, thin 20-year-old with very long fingers and hypermobile joints dies of a tearing aortic dissection. Elastic stain of the aorta shows sparse, fragmented elastic tissue. Which layer of the aortic wall is primarily defective?
  1. A. Tunica intima
  2. B. Internal elastic lamina
  3. C. Tunica media
  4. D. Tunica adventitia
  5. E. Vasa vasorum
AnswerC. Tunica media
WhyMarfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 mutation) weakens elastic fibers, because elastin is laid down on fibrillin microfibrils, and frees TGF-β, which activates MMPs that degrade elastic tissue. That tissue is concentrated in the tunica media of elastic arteries, so the aortic media fails → aneurysm and dissection. The IEL is a single sheet, not the elastic mass of the wall.
Key factMarfan syndrome → tunica media of elastic arteries (aorta)
  • Defect: fibrillin-1, the microfibril scaffold of elastic fibers (elastic fiber = elastin + fibrillin microfibrils); less TGF-β sequestration → MMPs degrade elastic tissue.
  • Histology: loss/fragmentation of elastic fibers in the media.
  • Result: aortic aneurysm and dissection (blood dissects into the weakened media).
  • On a labelled or numbered micrograph pick the thick middle elastic band between the thin luminal intima and the outer adventitia with its vasa vasorum.
Clues: tall, thin, long hypermobile fingers, family history of sudden "tearing" chest pain.

WhyIn aortic dissection blood under arterial pressure passes through an intimal tear and splits the tunica media, whose concentric elastic lamellae are the wall's main structural support. Key factAortic dissection: intimal tear → blood dissects within the media (often its outer third) along degenerated elastic lamellae.
  • The concentric elastic lamellae of the media are the main load-bearing component resisting systolic pressure; the outermost tunic is collagenous connective tissue (adventitia).
  • Causes: chronic hypertension, Marfan (fibrillin), other medial degeneration. "Tearing" chest pain to the back.
  • Image: a false lumen of blood inside the aortic wall, vs atherosclerosis = intimal plaque narrowing the lumen.

54unlocks 7TA ×21 not obvious
A 60-year-old smoker with hypertension and an LDL of 180 mg/dL has coronary artery disease. By the response-to-injury hypothesis taught in class, which event starts the process that produces their plaques?
  1. A. Proliferation of smooth muscle cells in the intima
  2. B. Proliferation of fibroblasts in the adventitia
  3. C. Formation of a collagen-rich fibrous cap
  4. D. Injury and dysfunction of endothelial cells
  5. E. Degeneration of elastic lamellae in the media
AnswerD. Injury and dysfunction of endothelial cells
WhyAtherogenesis begins with endothelial injury/dysfunction (hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, cigarette toxins), which raises permeability so LDL enters the intima and is oxidized; monocytes become macrophages and then foam cells; later smooth muscle cells migrate from the media into the intima and build the fibrous cap. SM proliferation and the cap are later steps.
Key factResponse-to-injury hypothesis (2026 interactive session): a chronic inflammatory healing response to endothelial injury, in this order:
  • Endothelial injury (hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, smoking) → ↑ permeability
  • LDL accumulates in the intima and is oxidized
  • Monocytes enter → macrophages engulf oxidized LDL → foam cells
  • Mediators and growth factors (PDGF) → smooth muscle cells migrate from the media into the intima and make matrix → fibrous cap over a lipid/necrotic core
  • Late: necrosis, calcification, plaque rupture, thrombosis, partial → complete occlusion

  • Ordering questions (LDL → foam cells → cap) and "source of foam cells" (macrophages) or "cells that build the fibrous cap" (smooth muscle).

  4. D. Cap: macrophages; foamy cells: endothelial cells

AnswerB. Cap: smooth muscle cells that migrated from the media; foamy cells: macrophages derived from monocytes
WhyMonocytes enter the intima and become macrophages that engulf oxidized LDL → foam cells. Growth factors then make smooth muscle cells migrate from the media into the intima, where they secrete collagen and matrix → the fibrous cap. Fibroblasts belong to the adventitia and pericytes to capillaries, not to plaques.
Key factWho is who among vessel-wall cells
  • Smooth muscle cell = the only cell of the media. Besides contracting it synthesizes elastin, collagen and proteoglycans (it makes the aortic lamellae). In atherosclerosis it migrates into the intima and builds the fibrous cap; in hypertension it hypertrophies. Nuclei in the media = smooth muscle cells.
  • Macrophage (from blood monocytes) engulfs oxidized LDL → foam cell (lipid-filled cells of the plaque core, with cholesterol clefts).
  • Endothelial cell: the lining; its injury starts atherogenesis, but it is not the cap or foam-cell source.
  • Fibroblast: adventitia, not the media; pericyte: capillaries and venules; neutrophil: acute inflammation, not plaques.
Course model (F3531:26): monocytes become macrophages and lipid-containing foam cells; smooth muscle cells migrate from the media and produce extracellular matrix. Smooth-muscle-derived foam cells exist in pathology texts, but the course and the TA key (TAG39) answer macrophages.

  • TA: plaque → intima; hypertension → media.

What it lets you eliminate

  • Cystic medial necrosis "in the tunica intima" is self-contradictory; atherosclerosis "in the media" or "adventitia" is wrong.
  • Marfan never targets the intima, arterioles or veins.

A high-power section of the aortic wall shows a single layer of flattened cells with thin, elongated nuclei facing the lumen. Beneath them is a narrow band of loose connective tissue that ends at the first elastic lamella. Which choice correctly names the lining cells and the band beneath them?
  1. A. Simple cuboidal endothelium; internal elastic membrane
  2. B. Simple squamous endothelium; subendothelial layer of the intima
  3. C. Mesothelium; subendothelial layer
  4. D. Mesothelium; tunica media
  5. E. Smooth muscle cells; subendothelial layer
AnswerB. Simple squamous endothelium; subendothelial layer of the intima
WhyEvery blood vessel is lined by endothelium, a simple squamous epithelium, and the loose connective tissue under it is the subendothelial layer. Together they make up the tunica intima. Mesothelium is also simple squamous, but it lines serous cavities like the pericardium and pleura, never a vessel lumen.
Key factEndothelium = simple squamous epithelium (flat cells, thin elongated nuclei) lining every blood vessel, capillary and lymphatic, and the heart (endocardium). Any vascular channel, even a hemangioma (strawberry birthmark), is lined by endothelial cells. Being so thin, it allows rapid exchange between blood and tissue.
Tunica intima = endothelium + basal lamina → subendothelial loose CT (with occasional smooth muscle) → internal elastic lamina (in muscular arteries). In the aorta the subendothelium is the pale band between the endothelium and the first elastic lamella.
Mesothelium (also simple squamous) lines serous cavities, not vessels.
What it unlocks: 4 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Rapid-fire micrograph of a vessel lining: 'what type of epithelium?' or 'top arrows are what cells? (be specific)' → simple squamous endothelial cells
  • Aorta at high power with a double arrow on the band under the lining → subendothelium (vs elastic lamella, internal elastic membrane, endothelium, media)
  • Clinical: benign blood-filled channels of a neonate's strawberry hemangioma are lined by which cells → endothelial cells

What it lets you eliminate

  • Mesothelial cells line serous cavities (epicardium, pleura), never a vessel lumen
  • Fibroblasts, smooth muscle and inflammatory cells sit beneath or around the lining; they never form it
  • No vessel is lined by cuboidal or stratified epithelium

Healthy endothelial cells release vasodilators such as nitric oxide but also vasoconstrictors such as endothelin, and they can both prevent and promote clotting and inflammation. Which statement best describes normal endothelial function?
  1. A. Only vasodilation, growth inhibition and anticoagulation; the opposite actions occur only in disease
  2. B. Recruitment of leukocytes only, making it purely proinflammatory
  3. C. A balance of opposing actions: dilation vs constriction, growth inhibition vs promotion, antithrombotic vs prothrombotic, anti- vs proinflammatory
  4. D. Gas exchange only, limited to capillaries
  5. E. A passive barrier with no role in vascular tone

WhyDr Bruno's endothelium slide shows a balance: dilatation, growth inhibition, antithrombosis and anti-inflammation on one side, and constriction, growth promotion, prothrombosis and proinflammation on the other. All eight are normal endothelial functions, so option A is the trap; disease is a shift in the balance, as in atherosclerosis.
Key factNormal endothelial function = a balance (Dr Bruno):
Dilatation vs Constriction
Growth inhibition vs Growth promotion
Antithrombosis vs Prothrombosis
Anti-inflammation vs Proinflammation
All eight are endothelial functions. The 2026 interactive session adds: selective permeability barrier; vascular tone (secretes vasodilators and vasoconstrictors); antithrombogenic surface under normal conditions; lets inflammatory and immune cells migrate into tissues; angiogenesis in development and repair. Endothelial injury and dysfunction start atherosclerosis (response-to-injury).

A small, round vessel has a narrow lumen with endothelial nuclei bulging into it. The endothelium sits directly on a ring of two layers of circular smooth muscle, and only a very thin layer of connective tissue surrounds it. No elastic lamellae are seen. What is this vessel?

WhyOne to three smooth muscle layers directly under the endothelium, a very thin adventitia and a lumen that is small for its wall = arteriole. A muscular artery has many smooth muscle layers and a prominent internal elastic lamina. Capillaries and venules have no complete muscle coat.
Key factArteriole (Dr Bruno): Intima = endothelium only (no subendothelial CT or smooth muscle); Media = 1-3 layers of smooth muscle; Adventitia = very thin CT.
Look: small, round vessel; narrow lumen, thick wall relative to the lumen; endothelial nuclei often bulge into the lumen. Any complete smooth-muscle ring, however thin, = arteriole (a 'smaller arteriole' still has muscle; a capillary has none).
vs muscular artery: many smooth muscle layers + prominent wavy internal elastic lamina
vs capillary: endothelium only
vs venule: wide lumen, thin wall, full of blood

During exercise, blood flow to the capillary beds of working skeletal muscle rises several-fold while gut flow falls. Which vessels are mainly responsible for this redistribution, and how?
  1. A. Elastic arteries, by elastic recoil that smooths pulse pressure
  2. B. Venules, by valves that prevent backflow
  3. C. Medium veins, by acting as blood reservoirs
  4. D. Capillaries, by contraction of their endothelial cells
  5. E. Arterioles, by changing smooth muscle tone to alter lumen radius and resistance
AnswerE. Arterioles, by changing smooth muscle tone to alter lumen radius and resistance
WhyArterioles are the resistance vessels, the primary site of vascular resistance. Autonomic and local control of their 1-3 smooth muscle layers changes lumen radius, which sets systemic blood pressure and how much blood enters each capillary bed. Elastic arteries are low-resistance conducting vessels, and capillaries have no muscle.
Key factArterioles = resistance vessels, 'the primary site of vascular resistance' (Dr Bruno).
Smooth muscle tone (autonomic + local metabolites) → lumen radius ↑ or ↓ → regulates systemic blood pressure and flow into capillary beds (they dilate in exercising muscle).
Hypertension → arteriolar wall thickening (smooth muscle proliferation) with a narrowed lumen.
Compare: elastic arteries = conducting, low resistance, recoil smooths pulse pressure; muscular arteries = distributing; capillaries = exchange; veins = blood reservoirs; postcapillary venules = leukocyte exit.

Capillaries

63unlocks 9TA ×2
In myocardium, a tiny channel between cardiac muscle fibers is lined by a single flattened endothelial cell on a basal lamina, has no smooth muscle or adventitia, and holds red cells in single file. What is it, and what is its main function?
  1. A. Capillary; exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes
  2. B. Venule; exit of leukocytes
  3. C. Small artery; distribution of blood
  4. D. Lymphatic capillary; drainage of interstitial fluid
  5. E. Arteriole; regulation of vascular resistance
AnswerA. Capillary; exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes
WhyA wall of endothelium only (plus basal lamina and pericytes), with no media or adventitia and a lumen just wide enough for one red cell, is a capillary, the exchange vessel. Even one smooth muscle ring would make it an arteriole. Lymphatic capillaries contain no red cells.
Key factCapillary (Dr Bruno): Intima = endothelium only (+ basal lamina); Media = none (only pericytes); Adventitia = none.
Diameter about one RBC → red cells pass in single file. Smallest vessel; fine detail needs EM.
Function: exchange vessels. The thin wall allows rapid exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes.
LM look: a thin pink endothelial tube with an elongated nucleus, running between muscle fibers or fat cells, or looping up into dermal papillae ('capillary loops'). One smooth muscle layer = arteriole; an empty thin channel with no RBCs = lymphatic.

An electron micrograph of a capillary shows thin endothelium perforated by many small pores, each spanned by a thin membrane. Beneath the endothelium is a basal lamina. Which choice correctly names the capillary and the two labelled features?
  1. A. Continuous capillary; marginal fold and basal lamina
  2. B. Sinusoid; tight junction and discontinuous basal lamina
  3. C. Fenestrated capillary; pore diaphragm and continuous basal lamina
  4. D. Fenestrated capillary; gap junction and basal lamina
  5. E. Fenestrated capillary; pore diaphragm and discontinuous basal lamina
AnswerC. Fenestrated capillary; pore diaphragm and continuous basal lamina
WhyPores (fenestrae) closed by thin diaphragms over a continuous basal lamina = fenestrated capillary. A discontinuous basal lamina is found only in sinusoids, which is the trap in option E. Marginal folds and tight junctions without pores mark a continuous capillary.
Key factContinuous: unbroken endothelium joined by tight junctions with marginal folds (small flaps of endothelial cytoplasm projecting into the lumen at cell junctions), pinocytotic vesicles, no fenestrae, continuous basal lamina; smallest diameter.
Fenestrated: endothelium with many pores (fenestrae) bridged by thin diaphragms; basal lamina still continuous; intermediate diameter.
Discontinuous = sinusoid: largest, irregular lumen; gaps between endothelial cells + large fenestrae; discontinuous basal lamina. The lab's sinusoid TEM is a liver sinusoid: a thin, gappy lining with hepatocyte microvilli in the space of Disse behind it; on SEM the fenestrae cluster into sieve plates (hepatic sinusoid). An SEM of a wall full of large irregular holes = sinusoid.
Pericytes occur on all types, so they never identify the type.
Several page key notes fix mis-assigned source keys (q144, q184, q227, q270, q328: continuous vs sinusoid answers that belonged to neighbouring slides); the answers here follow the key notes, which match the lab slides.

Explanation from the source
The answer is A: Continuous endothelial cells with continuous basal lamina. Three types of capillaries can be distinguished on the basis of their ultrastructural morphology: continuous, fenestrated, and discontinuous. Continuous capillaries have an uninterrupted endothelial lining, surrounded by a continuous layer of basal lamina. Endothelial cells are linked by tight junctions (zonula occludens). Continuous capillaries are found in the lungs, CNS, thymus, skeletal muscle, and bone. Fenestrated capillaries (choices C and D) have many small windows (fenestra) that facilitate the diffusion of biological molecules across the endothelium. The fenestrations may, or may not, be covered by a thin “diaphragm.” The basal lamina is continuous in fenestrated capillaries. Fenestrated capillaries with diaphragms are found in the intestines, endocrine organs, and kidney tubules (i.e., peritubular capillaries). Fenestrated capillaries without diaphragms facilitate the ultrafiltration of blood in the renal glomerulus. Discontinuous capillaries (also referred to as sinusoidal capillaries) display an incomplete endothelial lining and a fragmented basal lamina. These capillaries (choices B and E) facilitate communication between parenchymal cells and blood. Discontinuous capillaries are found in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Keywords: Capillaries, endothelial cells
How it follows from the main questionIgnore the cancer: the tissue is lung (alveolar septa), and lung capillaries are continuous → continuous endothelium with a continuous basal lamina (not fenestrated or sinusoidal).

66unlocks 2TA ×2
Compared with the fenestrated capillaries of a renal glomerulus, the sinusoids of the liver and bone marrow are specialized to:
  1. A. Regulate vascular resistance by smooth muscle contraction
  2. B. Filter fluid and small solutes while holding back cells and most proteins
  3. C. Allow maximal molecular exchange, passage of plasma proteins and movement of whole blood cells across the wall
  4. D. Prevent backflow with endothelial valves
  5. E. Restrict passage to lipid-soluble molecules only
AnswerC. Allow maximal molecular exchange, passage of plasma proteins and movement of whole blood cells across the wall
WhySinusoids (largest diameter, intercellular gaps, discontinuous basal lamina) allow maximal molecular exchange and movement of blood cells: new blood cells leave the marrow and plasma proteins cross in the liver. Fenestrated capillaries (option B) filter fluid and small solutes quickly but keep cells and proteins in. Continuous capillaries (option E, the brain) are the most restrictive.
Key factPermeability rises continuous → fenestrated → sinusoid.
Continuous: most selective; tight junctions; transport by pinocytotic vesicles. Brain = blood-brain barrier = lowest permeability (only lipid-soluble drugs like alcohol, nicotine and caffeine cross easily).
Fenestrated: rapid exchange and filtration of water and small solutes (hormones leaving endocrine cells, absorbed nutrients in the gut, glomerular filtrate) while retaining cells and most proteins.
Sinusoid: 'greater diameter than most capillaries; maximal molecular exchange and movement of blood cells' (Dr Bruno) → plasma proteins and whole cells cross (new blood cells enter the circulation from marrow).
All capillaries are exchange vessels. None regulate resistance, since they have no smooth muscle.

WhyA cell outside the endothelium but inside its basal lamina is a pericyte, while the nucleus that bulges into the lumen belongs to the endothelial cell. Fibroblasts and macrophages lie outside the basal lamina.
Key factPericytes: small cells with long processes wrapped around capillaries and postcapillary venules, outside the endothelium but enclosed in (sharing) its basal lamina.
Nature: contractile mesenchymal adult stem cells → can become smooth muscle cells or fibroblasts and help vessel repair; they support and maintain endothelial cells and limit permeability (they surround the brain's continuous capillaries at the BBB).
EM: the endothelial nucleus bulges into the lumen (it forms the wall); the pericyte nucleus sits outside, hugging the endothelium. LM: elongated cells ('P') on the outer capillary surface.

Two small vessels lie side by side. Vessel 1 has a wide, oval lumen packed with red cells and a wall of endothelium with a few pericytes. Vessel 2 has a narrow, round lumen with bulging endothelial nuclei and a ring of smooth muscle. Which identification is correct?
  1. A. 1 = arteriole, 2 = venule
  2. B. 1 = venule, 2 = arteriole
  3. C. 1 = lymphatic vessel, 2 = arteriole
  4. D. 1 = capillary, 2 = small artery
  5. E. 1 = venule, 2 = capillary
AnswerB. 1 = venule, 2 = arteriole
WhyVenules have a large diameter and relatively thin wall (endothelium + pericytes, later a few smooth muscle cells) and usually contain blood. Arterioles have a narrow lumen and thick wall of 1-3 smooth muscle layers. A lymphatic would also be thin-walled, but it would have no red cells.
Key factVenules (Dr Bruno): between capillaries and veins; large diameter, relatively thin wall. Postcapillary venule wall = endothelium + pericytes; muscular venules add 1-2 smooth muscle layers. Usually full of RBCs, with an oval or irregular lumen.
Arteriole: small round lumen, thick wall relative to lumen (1-3 smooth muscle layers), endothelial nuclei bulge in.
Rule: in the same field, the wider, thinner-walled, blood-filled vessel is the venule or vein, and the small thick muscular ring is the arteriole. Venules have a larger lumen than arterioles. (Thin-walled + no RBCs + irregular = lymphatic; the smallest endothelial tube = capillary.)
The lecture gives venule size inconsistently (F0717:26: venule <0.01 mm; F0717:40: <0.001 mm). No practice question asks it, but check it if the TAs' 'know vein sizes' tip matters.

In a microvascular bed, rings of a few smooth muscle cells sit where true capillaries branch off a metarteriole. When they contract, blood bypasses the capillaries through the thoroughfare channel. What are these rings, and what do they do?
  1. A. Precapillary sphincters; act as switches that regulate blood flow into the capillary bed
  2. B. Venous valves; prevent backflow from veins into capillaries
  3. C. Capillary endothelial cells; contract to close the lumen
  4. D. Postcapillary venules; regulate leukocyte exit
  5. E. Pericytes; form the blood-brain barrier
AnswerA. Precapillary sphincters; act as switches that regulate blood flow into the capillary bed
WhyPrecapillary sphincters are a few circular smooth muscle cells at the origin of capillaries (from arterioles or metarterioles). Contracting or relaxing them switches perfusion of each capillary bed off or on. Capillary endothelium and venules have no such muscular control.
Key factMicrovascular bed = arteriole → metarteriole → true capillaries → postcapillary venule (+ a thoroughfare channel).
Precapillary sphincters = rings of a few smooth muscle cells where capillaries leave the arteriole or metarteriole. Relaxed → capillary bed perfused; contracted → blood bypasses the bed via the thoroughfare channel. They directly regulate flow into the capillary bed ('switches').
Arterioles set overall resistance and distribute flow between organs; the sphincters fine-tune each bed. If a question asks what directly controls flow into a particular capillary bed and offers both, pick precapillary sphincters.

In which arrangement does blood pass through two capillary beds in series, as when blood from the intestinal capillaries travels in a vein to the sinusoids of the liver?
  1. A. Portal system
  2. B. Thoroughfare channel
  3. C. Arteriovenous shunt
  4. D. Vasa vasorum
  5. E. Simple pathway
AnswerA. Portal system
WhyA portal system runs artery → capillary bed → portal vessel → second capillary bed → vein, and the hepatic portal vein carries gut blood to the liver sinusoids. An AV shunt skips the capillary bed entirely (e.g. the glomus body), and a simple pathway has only one bed.
Key factDr Bruno's three pathways:
Simple: artery → arteriole → capillary bed → venule → vein.
Arteriovenous shunt: arteriole joins the venule directly, bypassing the capillary bed (e.g. the glomus body in fingertip dermis, for thermoregulation).
Portal system: capillary bed → portal vessel → second capillary bed → vein. Venous portal: liver (gut capillaries → hepatic portal vein → liver sinusoids). Arterial portal: kidney (afferent arteriole → glomerular capillaries → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries or vasa recta).
Afferent = arriving (moving toward a structure); efferent = exiting. The glomerulus is fed by the afferent arteriole and drained by the efferent arteriole. In a lymph node, afferent lymphatics pierce the capsule into the subcapsular sinus, and efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum.
The glomus body, renal glomerulus and lymph node questions (q237, q238, q243) are only partly CP1 material; the TAs stressed knowing afferent vs efferent arterioles.

What it lets you eliminate

  • 'Afferent' never means leaving and 'efferent' never means arriving

Lymphatics

72unlocks 5TA ×2
In connective tissue next to a small artery and vein is a vessel with an extremely thin endothelial wall and an irregular, partly collapsed lumen. The lumen contains pale pink fluid and a few lymphocytes but no red blood cells, and thin paired leaflets project into it. What is this vessel?
  1. A. Medium-sized vein
  2. B. Venule
  3. C. Capillary
  4. D. Arteriole
  5. E. Lymphatic vessel
AnswerE. Lymphatic vessel
WhyLymphatic vessels have thinner walls and less distinct layers than blood vessels of similar size. Their lumens are irregular or collapsed, they carry pale proteinaceous lymph with lymphocytes and no red cells, and they have thin valves. A venule is also thin-walled but contains RBCs.
Key factLymphatic vessel look: very thin wall (endothelium with little CT or smooth muscle; layers indistinct), poorly defined basement membrane, irregular, often collapsed or slit-like lumen, lightly staining pale pink proteinaceous lymph (sometimes with lymphocytes), NO red blood cells, and valves (thin paired infoldings of intima covered by endothelium).
Discriminator: a venule is thin-walled too but has RBCs and a rounder lumen; a vein has a media and blood; an arteriole has a muscular ring.
Seen beside arteries and veins in CT, and as large thin channels at the lymph node hilum.
q186's printed key says 'blind ended (right side), valve'. Per the page key note, no blind end is visible; the identifying clues are the very thin wall, the valve and the absence of RBCs.

Which feature distinguishes lymphatic capillaries from blood capillaries?
  1. A. They collapse when interstitial pressure rises
  2. B. They lack an endothelial lining
  3. C. They are open-ended and have very thick walls
  4. D. They are blind-ended tubes of overlapping endothelial cells without tight junctions, with an incomplete basal lamina and anchoring filaments
  5. E. They are less permeable than blood capillaries
AnswerD. They are blind-ended tubes of overlapping endothelial cells without tight junctions, with an incomplete basal lamina and anchoring filaments
WhyLymphatic capillaries are close-ended (blind-ended), very thin tubes. Their overlapping endothelial cells lack tight junctions, the basal lamina is incomplete, and anchoring filaments hold them open. Interstitial fluid and proteins therefore enter easily: they are more permeable than blood capillaries and stay open, rather than collapsing, when tissue pressure rises.
Key factLymphatic capillaries (Dr Bruno + 2026 lab): close-ended (blind-ended), very thin endothelial tubes. The endothelial cells overlap and lack tight junctions; the basal lamina is incomplete or discontinuous. Interstitial fluid enters through openings between endothelial cells; anchoring filaments (collagen and elastin) hold the tubes open as tissue swells; endothelial flaps stop backflow.
→ more permeable than blood capillaries (they take up proteins, debris and chylomicrons).
Found in most tissues but absent from the CNS (and bone marrow).
They begin blind and join into valved collecting vessels.
