Lymph from the right foot returns to the bloodstream. Which statement about its route and propulsion is correct?
  1. A. It drains to the right lymphatic duct, propelled by a thick muscular media in the lymphatic wall
  2. B. It drains to the right lymphatic duct; lymphatic vessels have no valves
  3. C. It drains to the thoracic duct; flow depends on valves and compression by contracting skeletal muscle and surrounding tissues
  4. D. It drains to the thoracic duct, driven mainly by arterial pressure transmitted through the capillaries
  5. E. It enters the inferior vena cava directly through venous valves
AnswerC. It drains to the thoracic duct; flow depends on valves and compression by contracting skeletal muscle and surrounding tissues
WhyThe thoracic duct drains both legs, the abdomen and the left upper body. Only the right upper body (right arm and the right side of the head, neck and thorax) drains to the right lymphatic duct. Thin-walled lymphatics move lymph by valves plus external compression from contracting skeletal muscle and surrounding tissue.
Key factDrainage: lymph → lymph nodes → larger lymphatics → back to the blood via the thoracic duct (both lower limbs, abdomen, left arm, left side of head and thorax) or the right lymphatic duct (right arm and right side of head, neck and thorax only).
Propulsion: lymphatic walls are thin with little muscle, so flow depends on external force: compression by contracting skeletal muscle and surrounding tissues, plus valves (as in veins) that keep flow one-way.
Valves are found in lymph vessels and veins; arteries, arterioles and capillaries have none (and the inferior vena cava has none).

Another develops non-pitting arm swelling with orange-peel skin months after a mastectomy with axillary lymph node removal. Both conditions result from obstruction or loss of which vessels?

Airway organization

77unlocks 18TA ×3
Tracing the airway from the nose into the lung, which segment is the LAST one of the conducting portion?
  1. A. Respiratory bronchiole
  2. B. Alveolar duct
  3. C. Terminal bronchiole
  4. D. Large bronchiole
  5. E. Segmental bronchus
AnswerC. Terminal bronchiole
WhyThe conducting portion runs from the nasal cavity to the terminal bronchioles, and no alveoli open from a terminal bronchiole's wall. The respiratory bronchiole is the first segment with alveoli in its wall, so it starts the respiratory portion; segmental bronchi and large bronchioles conduct air but are not the most distal.
Key factConducting portion (conditions and moves air, no gas exchange): nasal cavity → nasopharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles (last conducting segment).
Respiratory portion (gas exchange): respiratory bronchioles (first segment with alveoli in the wall) → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs → alveoli; type I and II pneumocytes belong here.
So 'gas exchange occurs in terminal bronchioles' = false, and 'the respiratory portion begins at' = respiratory bronchioles.

Which statement about the divisions of the respiratory tract is correct?

  2. B. The respiratory portion includes the trachea and bronchi
  3. C. The upper and lower tracts correspond exactly to the conducting and respiratory portions
  4. D. The upper/lower boundary lies between the false and true vocal cords
  5. E. The larynx is the first structure of the lower respiratory tract
AnswerE. The larynx is the first structure of the lower respiratory tract
WhyAnatomically the upper tract is the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses and pharynx, and the lower tract begins at the larynx (boundary = pharynx/larynx). This does not match the functional split: the lower tract holds both conducting airways (larynx to terminal bronchioles) and the respiratory portion, and the terminal/respiratory bronchiole junction is the functional, not the anatomic, boundary.
Key factTwo different ways to divide the tract:
  • Anatomic: upper = nasal cavity, sinuses, pharynx; lower = larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs. Boundary = pharynx | larynx.
  • Functional/histologic: conducting = nasal cavity → terminal bronchioles; respiratory = respiratory bronchioles → alveoli. Boundary = terminal | respiratory bronchiole.
They do not correspond: the conducting portion spans the whole upper tract and much of the lower tract.
What it unlocks: 2 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • 'The transition from the upper to the lower respiratory tract is located between…' (pharynx and larynx; distractors terminal/respiratory bronchioles, false/true vocal cords, trachea/large bronchi, middle/superior concha)
  • Figure 17-1 question: 'do the 2 anatomic divisions correspond to the 2 functional portions?' (no)

What it lets you eliminate

  • Terminal vs respiratory bronchiole is the functional boundary, not upper/lower
  • False vs true vocal cords and trachea vs bronchi are not boundaries of either scheme

Which pairing of an olfactory epithelial cell with its role is correct?
  1. A. Brush cell: replaces worn-out olfactory neurons
  2. B. Olfactory neuron: bipolar receptor cell with non-motile cilia on its dendritic knob
  3. C. Basal cell: bipolar neuron whose axon forms CN I
  4. D. Supporting cell: detects odorants with motile cilia
  5. E. Goblet cell: moistens the olfactory surface
AnswerB. Olfactory neuron: bipolar receptor cell with non-motile cilia on its dendritic knob
WhySmell is detected by olfactory neurons, true bipolar neurons with one dendrite ending in a knob of long non-motile cilia (odorant receptors) and one axon through the cribriform plate (CN I). Supporting cells are glia-like cells with microvilli, basal cells are the stem cells, and olfactory epithelium has no goblet cells.
Key factOlfactory epithelium (pseudostratified, no goblet cells), 3 cells:
  • Olfactory (receptor) neurons = bipolar neurons, the cells that detect odorants: their dendrites reach the luminal surface and end in knobs with non-motile cilia bearing odorant receptors; axons → lamina propria → cribriform plate → olfactory nerve (CN I) → olfactory bulb. True neurons that are continually replaced.
  • Supporting (sustentacular) cells: tall, microvilli, ion channels; mechanical and metabolic support = neuroglia-like; the most numerous cell
  • Basal cells: stem cells that replace neurons and supporting cells

Practice Q364Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
In the tissue depicted in this micrograph, the surface facing the lumen contains [blank 1] . The cells where these projections originate are [blank 2] . The middle of this slide shows the [blank 3] , which produce mucus to coat epithelial surface.
  1. Blank 1: nerve dendrites | cilia | stereocilia | nerve axons
  2. Blank 2: pseudounipolar neurons | bipolar neurons | goblet cells | columnar epithelial cells
  3. Blank 3: club cells | goblet cells | striated ducts | bowman’s glands
AnswerBlank 1 → nerve dendrites
Blank 2 → bipolar neurons
Blank 3 → bowman’s glands
WhyThe luminal processes are dendrites (knobs with non-motile cilia) of bipolar olfactory neurons, and the lamina propria glands are serous Bowman's glands.
Explanation from the source
This is a medium power view of the olfactory epithelium that contains a meshwork of sustentacular microvilli and olfactory non-motile cilia on the surface. The epithelium is pseudostratified columnar and it is hard to differentiate between the olfactory receptor cells, sustentacular cells and basal epithelial cells. However, the nuclei of the sustentacular cells tend to be in the top portion of the layer, the nuclei of the olfactory receptor cells tend to be in the middle portion, and the nuclei of the basal epithelial cells tend to be in the bottom portion. One can also see the an afferent nerve bundle. The dendrites of the olfactory neurons are sometimes called "non-motile cilia", due to the fact that at light microscopy they resemble cilia. However, they are in fact dendrites.

Below the epithelial layer there is a lamina propria. This lamina propria is composed of connective tissue, and is where we find the bowman’s glands, which produce mucus to trap odorants and eventually wash them away. Below the bowman’s glands is a bundle of nerves, formed by the axons of the bipolar neurons, which will run through the cribriform plate to the olfactory cortex via the olfactory nerve.
How it follows from the main questionSurface = dendrites (knobs with cilia) of bipolar neurons. The glands are Bowman's glands; don't pick goblet cells because the stem says 'mucus': olfactory epithelium has no goblet cells.

After COVID, one patient's smell returns within months. Another patient fractures the ethmoid bone and never recovers smell. Which pair best explains the two outcomes?
  1. A. Supporting cells regenerate; supporting cells are crushed
  2. B. Goblet cells recover; Bowman's glands are destroyed
  3. C. Brush cells regenerate; olfactory bulb neurons divide
  4. D. Basal stem cells replace olfactory neurons; olfactory axons are sheared at the cribriform plate
  5. E. Olfactory neurons divide; the nasal vestibule is scarred
AnswerD. Basal stem cells replace olfactory neurons; olfactory axons are sheared at the cribriform plate
WhyBasal cells are stem cells that replace olfactory neurons (every 1–2 months), so smell lost to a cold, COVID or toxic fumes comes back. The neurons' axons pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid; a fracture shears them and scarring blocks regrowth, so that anosmia is permanent. Mature olfactory neurons don't divide themselves.
Key fact
  • Temporary anosmia (URI, COVID, toxic fumes, mild trauma): only receptor neurons are damaged → basal stem cells replace them (normally every 1–2 months; supporting cells less often) → smell returns
  • Permanent anosmia: cribriform plate (ethmoid) fracture tears the olfactory axons (CN I filaments) → neurons disconnected from the brain
TA: 'smell is restored as long as we have basal cells, and as long as they stay connected to the brain.'

An airway lining shows tall cells with apical cilia, pale goblet cells, and nuclei at several heights, all resting on a thick basement membrane. How is it classified?

  3. C. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
  4. D. Transitional epithelium

AnswerC. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
WhyNuclei at several levels while every cell touches the basement membrane = pseudostratified; add cilia, goblet cells and a thick BM and it is respiratory epithelium. It only looks stratified because the basal cells don't reach the lumen.
Key factRespiratory epithelium = pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells: nuclei at different heights, all cells on one thick basement membrane, apical motile cilia, pale goblet cells, small basal cells along the BM.
Lines the 'respiratory tract': nasal cavity (respiratory region), paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, larynx (except vocal folds and lingual epiglottis), trachea, bronchi. A nasal polyp keeps this lining. Not to confuse: pseudostratified with stereocilia = epididymis.

What is the principal function of the most numerous cell type in tracheal epithelium?
  1. A. Secreting mucin glycoproteins into the lumen
  2. B. Secreting peptide hormones
  3. C. Coordinated beating that moves mucus and trapped particles toward the pharynx
  4. D. Detecting odorants
  5. E. Absorbing fluid by pinocytosis
AnswerC. Coordinated beating that moves mucus and trapped particles toward the pharynx
WhyThe most numerous cells are ciliated columnar cells, each with 250–300 motile cilia (9+2 microtubule axonemes). Their coordinated beating moves the mucus blanket toward the pharynx, the mucociliary escalator. Mucin comes from goblet cells, odorant detection from non-motile olfactory cilia, hormones from small granule cells.
Key factCiliated columnar cells (most numerous): 250–300 motile cilia each = 9+2 microtubule axoneme with dynein arms; long, unbranched; beat in coordination → move mucus and trapped particles toward the oropharynx (mucociliary escalator). It also carries out alveolar macrophages (dust cells) that have phagocytosed inhaled particles.
Compare: stereocilia and brush border = actin-cored microvilli (non-motile); olfactory cilia = non-motile receptors. Motile cilia protect the airway; the digestive tract has none.

Which apical specialization is correctly matched with its structure and the effect of its loss?
  1. A. Motile airway cilia: carry odorant receptors; loss causes anosmia
  2. B. Olfactory cilia: non-motile, carry odorant receptors; loss causes anosmia
  3. C. Brush-border microvilli: dynein-driven beating; loss causes bronchiectasis
  4. D. Brush-cell microvilli: sweep mucus toward the pharynx; loss causes chronic sinusitis
  5. E. Stereocilia: 9+2 microtubules that beat to move sperm; loss causes male infertility
AnswerB. Olfactory cilia: non-motile, carry odorant receptors; loss causes anosmia
WhyOlfactory cilia on the neurons' dendritic knobs are long and non-motile; they hold the odorant receptors, so losing them causes anosmia. Motile 9+2 cilia with dynein arms move mucus (their failure → infections, plus infertility through sperm flagella), while stereocilia and microvilli are actin-cored, non-motile projections that never beat.
Key factFour look-alike apical projections:
  • Motile cilia (airway ciliated cells; also oviduct): long, unbranched, 9+2 microtubule axoneme + dynein arms on a basal body; beat → mucociliary clearance. Defect (PCD/Kartagener) → sinusitis, otitis, bronchiectasis; sperm flagella share the axoneme → infertility
  • Olfactory cilia: long, non-motile, on bipolar-neuron dendritic knobs; carry the odorant receptors → loss = anosmia
  • Stereocilia: long, often branched actin-cored microvilli, non-motile; epididymis/ductus deferens (absorption) and inner-ear hair cells; never in the airway
  • Microvilli: short actin cores (fimbrin/villin); intestinal brush border (absorption; loss → malabsorption, celiac) and the blunt tuft of airway brush cells (chemosensory)
Only motile cilia move mucus; only olfactory cilia smell.
Stereocilia and intestinal microvilli are Foundations (epithelium unit) facts; the CP1 practice questions use them only as distractors. The motile (respiratory) vs non-motile (olfactory) cilia contrast is stated on the 2025 review slide F1262:3.

96unlocks 8TA ×11 not obvious
Electron microscopy of airway cilia from a boy with recurrent sinusitis shows a normal 9+2 microtubule pattern, yet the cilia do not beat. Which component is most likely defective?
  1. A. Nuclear lamins
  2. B. Actin filaments
  3. C. Basal bodies
  4. D. Dynein arms
  5. E. Tubulin polymerization
AnswerD. Dynein arms
WhyCilia move because dynein arms (ATPase motors) slide the doublet microtubules of the 9+2 axoneme. In primary ciliary dyskinesia (DNAI1/DNAH5 mutations) the cilia are present with a normal-looking 9+2 layout but are immotile. Actin and lamins aren't in the axoneme, and absent basal bodies or failed tubulin polymerization would mean no cilia at all.
Key factMotile cilium = axoneme of 9+2 microtubules (9 doublets + central pair) with dynein arms (the motor), radial spokes, nexin.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener): mutations such as DNAI1, DNAH5 → defective dynein arms → cilia and sperm flagella present but immotile → persistent respiratory infections and infertility.
'Which structure is affected?' = cilia / microtubules / 9+2 axoneme / dynein arms; never actin, intermediate filaments, lamins, microvilli or stereocilia.

A bronchial biopsy from a patient with a 40-pack-year history shows patches where the lining is several layers of flattened cells without cilia or goblet cells. What has happened?
  1. A. Invasive carcinoma, irreversible by definition
  2. B. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar → stratified squamous (squamous metaplasia)
  3. C. Columnar → transitional epithelium (urothelial metaplasia)
  4. D. Goblet cells have turned into type I pneumocytes
  5. E. Stratified squamous → pseudostratified columnar (columnar metaplasia)
AnswerB. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar → stratified squamous (squamous metaplasia)
WhyChronic smoke immobilizes cilia and injures the lining, and the basal stem cells switch to a sturdier stratified squamous epithelium = squamous metaplasia. Losing ciliated and goblet cells abolishes mucociliary clearance; the change is still reversible and is not carcinoma, though dysplasia can follow. The reverse direction (squamous → columnar) is the esophageal Barrett pattern.
Key factSquamous metaplasia (smoking, air pollution): pseudostratified ciliated columnar → stratified squamous (lab shorthand: 'columnar to squamous').
Mechanism: airway basal (stem) cells redifferentiate into squamous cells. Consequence: no cilia or goblet cells → impaired mucociliary clearance → infections; can progress to dysplasia → squamous cell carcinoma.
TAG74 keys D 'Columnar to Squamous' but also offers F 'Pseudo to Squamous'. The lecture/lab wording (F3532:32) is 'pseudostratified ciliated columnar to stratified squamous', so F is just as defensible; the TA key follows the lab shorthand on F1264:29 ('columnar to squamous'). On the exam, choose whichever option names the change from (pseudostratified) columnar to squamous.

WhyMetaplasia = one mature cell type replaced by another mature type after chronic injury (squamous in smokers' airways; columnar in reflux esophagus). Key factMetaplasia: reversible replacement of one fully differentiated cell type by another, sturdier one after repeated insult (TA: 'one mature cell type to another mature cell type').
Examples: airway ciliated columnar → stratified squamous (smoking); esophagus squamous → columnar (reflux).
Reversible if the stimulus stops; persistent injury → dysplasia → carcinoma. Hyperplasia = ↑ cell number; dysplasia = disordered atypia; neoplasia = autonomous growth.

  • Local immunity: secretory component of IgA, antimicrobial peptides (lysozyme), cytokines

During an asthma attack, why do bronchioles narrow more than bronchi?
  1. A. Bronchioles lack cartilage and have a proportionately thick smooth muscle layer
  2. B. Bronchioles are lined by thick stratified squamous epithelium
  3. C. Bronchioles have more seromucous glands
  4. D. Bronchioles have complete cartilage rings that constrict
  5. E. Bronchioles have no smooth muscle, so they collapse passively
AnswerA. Bronchioles lack cartilage and have a proportionately thick smooth muscle layer
WhyBronchioles have no cartilage (and no glands) to hold them open and a relatively thick, well-developed smooth muscle layer, so bronchospasm after mast-cell degranulation can nearly close the lumen. Epinephrine and β2 agonists relax that smooth muscle.
Key factAsthma attack = bronchospasm of bronchiolar smooth muscle: specific antigen → mast cell degranulation (mucosa/BALT; histamine, leukotrienes) → bronchoconstriction + edema + mucus.
Bronchioles suffer most because they have no cartilage and a proportionately thick smooth muscle layer.
Treatment: β2 agonists (salbutamol) / epinephrine act directly on airway smooth muscle → relaxation → wider lumen. Among airway segments the terminal bronchiole (conducting, no cartilage) is the asthma target, not alveoli or alveolar ducts.

Contrast: emphysema = alveolar wall destruction; hyaline membrane disease = surfactant deficit.

A biopsy of an airway wall contains a plate of hyaline cartilage. It could have come from any of the following EXCEPT:

WhyHyaline cartilage is found in the larynx, the trachea (C-rings) and all bronchi (rings, then plates), and it ends with the bronchi. Bronchioles, terminal and respiratory bronchioles and everything distal have no cartilage and no glands, so a cartilage-containing section can never be a bronchiole.
Key factWhere cartilage is (and isn't):
  • Larynx: hyaline (thyroid, cricoid) + elastic (epiglottis)

  • Bronchioles → alveoli: none (and no glands)
Rule: cartilage ± seromucous glands = trachea or bronchus; no cartilage + no glands + smooth muscle = bronchiole. 'Conducting = cartilage + conduction; respiratory = exchange, no cartilage.'

  1. A. Vestibular (false) vocal fold: pseudostratified ciliated columnar
  2. B. Terminal bronchiole: pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells

The other pairs are right: skin in the outer vestibule, squamous on the lingual epiglottis (and true cords), respiratory epithelium on the false cords, simple squamous in alveolar ducts.
Key factLining, top → bottom:
  • Keratinized SS: outer nasal vestibule (skin, vibrissae)
  • Nonkeratinized SS: the two airway SS sites = true vocal folds and lingual/upper epiglottis

  • Simple ciliated columnar → cuboidal: bronchioles → terminal bronchioles (club cells, no goblet cells); respiratory bronchioles cuboidal between alveoli
  • Simple squamous: alveolar ducts, sacs, alveoli (type I cells)
So goblet cells + pseudostratified lining = trachea/bronchus level; an abrupt SS/respiratory junction with skeletal muscle = larynx.

As bronchi branch into smaller bronchi and then bronchioles, which change occurs?
  1. A. Smooth muscle disappears before the terminal bronchioles
  2. B. Goblet cells and glands become more numerous

AnswerE. Cartilage, glands and goblet cells dwindle and disappear, while smooth muscle stays prominent and elastic fibers persist
WhyDown the tree cartilage, glands and goblet cells shrink and are gone by the bronchioles, and the epithelium shortens (pseudostratified → simple columnar → cuboidal). Key factTable 19.1, trachea → alveoli:
  • Goblet cells: fade out in the bronchi (a few in the largest bronchioles, none in terminal bronchioles)
  • Glands and hyaline cartilage: end with the bronchi (last cartilage = bronchi)
  • Epithelium: pseudostratified ciliated columnar through the bronchi (last 'respiratory epithelium' = bronchi) → simple ciliated columnar → cuboidal in bronchioles (change at bronchus → bronchiole)
  • Cilia: persist into respiratory bronchioles; smooth muscle: prominent in bronchioles, persists to alveolar-duct openings
  • Elastic fibers: all the way into the alveoli → the component that increases proportionally
The 2026 lab slide F3532:15 labels the large bronchiole's epithelium 'respiratory epithelium' (it is ciliated, but simple columnar), and Lippincott (q450's explanation) says larger bronchioles have typical respiratory epithelium. Which feature is the main structural reason the lung can exchange O2 and CO2 efficiently?
  1. A. Capillaries of the interalveolar septa lying directly against the alveolar air spaces
  2. B. Repeated branching of the bronchial tree
  3. C. Dual (pulmonary and bronchial) arterial supply
  4. D. Pulmonary veins running alongside the bronchioles
  5. E. Smooth-muscle knobs at the openings of alveolar ducts
AnswerA. Capillaries of the interalveolar septa lying directly against the alveolar air spaces
WhyAir in an alveolus is separated from blood in the septal pulmonary capillaries by only a few hundred nanometres, so the close association of alveolar spaces and pulmonary capillaries is the basis of diffusion. A dual blood supply and branching are true but do not explain exchange; pulmonary veins run in the interlobular septa, not with the bronchioles.
Key factGas exchange begins in respiratory bronchioles (first alveoli), but the alveoli are the major site (about 300 million, huge surface).
Structural basis: each interalveolar septum is a dense capillary plexus sandwiched between alveolar air spaces, so alveolar air lies a fraction of a micrometre from capillary blood = close association of alveolar spaces and pulmonary capillaries.

A lung section shows a small airway with no cartilage or glands, lined by simple cuboidal cells including dome-shaped nonciliated cells, with a thin band of smooth muscle. Its wall is repeatedly interrupted by thin-walled alveoli opening directly into the lumen. What is this airway?
  1. A. Respiratory bronchiole

AnswerA. Respiratory bronchiole

Key factTerminal bronchiole (last conducting): simple cuboidal (some ciliated) with many club cells, 1–2 layers of smooth muscle, no cartilage, no glands, no goblet cells; complete wall with no alveoli opening into it; feeds two or more respiratory bronchioles.
Respiratory bronchiole (first respiratory): same cuboidal/club-cell lining (some cilia) plus smooth muscle bundles, but the wall is interrupted by alveoli opening into the lumen, so gas exchange begins here.
The one discriminator: alveoli in the wall. Cilia, club cells and smooth muscle are shared, glands and cartilage are absent from both.

In a low-power lung field, an elongated air passage has no continuous wall of its own: its sides are a row of alveolar openings whose rims carry small knobs of smooth muscle, and it ends in a blind space surrounded by a cluster of alveoli. What is the elongated passage?
  1. A. Alveolus
  2. B. Alveolar sac
  3. C. Alveolar duct
  4. D. Terminal bronchiole
  5. E. Respiratory bronchiole
AnswerC. Alveolar duct
WhyA corridor whose 'wall' is entirely alveolar openings with smooth-muscle knobs at the rims is an alveolar duct. The blind space it ends in is an alveolar sac; a respiratory bronchiole still has stretches of cuboidal-lined wall between scattered alveoli.
Key factSequence: terminal bronchiole → respiratory bronchiole → alveolar duct → alveolar sac → alveolus.
  • Respiratory bronchiole: a real wall (cuboidal + club cells, smooth muscle) with scattered alveoli
  • Alveolar duct: long 'hallway' with no wall of its own, lined by alveolar openings; smooth-muscle knobs at the rims of the openings (the last smooth muscle in the tree)
  • Alveolar sac: blind common space at the end of a duct into which a cluster of alveoli opens ('room')
  • Alveolus: one small pocket bounded by thin interalveolar septa; opens into a respiratory bronchiole, duct or sac

Which statement about the epithelium lining the alveoli is correct?
  1. A. It is mostly type II cells, which cover most of the alveolar surface
  2. B. It is pseudostratified columnar with goblet cells
  3. C. It is stratified squamous to resist friction from airflow
  4. D. It is simple cuboidal with cilia that sweep debris toward the bronchioles
  5. E. It is a simple squamous epithelium made mostly of thin type I cells that cover about 95% of the surface and do not divide
AnswerE. It is a simple squamous epithelium made mostly of thin type I cells that cover about 95% of the surface and do not divide
WhyAlveoli are lined by a simple squamous epithelium: thin type I pneumocytes cover about 95% of the surface (gas exchange) and cannot divide, while cuboidal type II cells are more numerous but cover only about 5%. Alveoli have no cilia and no goblet cells.
Key factType I pneumocyte: extremely thin squamous cell (cytoplasm as thin as ~25 nm), flat dark nucleus, covers ~95% of the alveolar surface; function = gas exchange, forms the alveolar side of the blood-air barrier; joined by occluding (tight) junctions; cannot divide (replaced by type II cells).
Alveolar lining = simple squamous epithelium of type I + type II pneumocytes; no cilia, no goblet cells.

A severe viral pneumonia selectively destroys one alveolar cell type, and the patient's alveoli then tend to collapse at end-expiration. Which cell was lost?
  1. A. Type I pneumocyte
  2. B. Type II pneumocyte
  3. C. Club cell
  4. D. Alveolar macrophage
  5. E. Goblet cell
AnswerB. Type II pneumocyte
WhyType II pneumocytes make and secrete surfactant; without it surface tension rises and alveoli collapse. Type I cells do gas exchange, macrophages phagocytose (they clear surfactant, not make it), and club and goblet cells are airway cells.
Key factType II pneumocyte (septal cell, great alveolar cell): cuboidal, rounded cell in the alveolar wall, often at septal junctions, round nucleus, foamy cytoplasm (lamellar bodies), apical microvilli; more numerous than type I cells but covers only ~5% of the surface.
Function: synthesizes, stores and secretes surfactant, which lowers surface tension so alveoli stay open; also the alveolar stem cell.
The only alveolar surfactant source: not type I cells, club cells, goblet cells, macrophages or 'pores of Kohn'. Loss of type II cells → ↑ alveolar tendency to collapse.

Rule of thumb: flat in the wall = type I; plump in the wall = type II; plump and free in the lumen = macrophage.

A TEM shows a cuboidal alveolar cell containing membrane-bound granules, 100–400 nm across, filled with closely stacked, onion-like membrane lamellae. What do these granules contain?
  1. A. Platelet dense-granule contents (ADP, calcium)

WhyGranules of stacked membrane lamellae are lamellar bodies, the storage organelle for surfactant (DPPC and other phospholipids, cholesterol, surfactant proteins), unique to type II pneumocytes and released by exocytosis. Serotonin and dense-core granules belong to neuroendocrine cells and platelets, mucin granules to goblet cells.
Key factLamellar body = membrane-bound granule (100–400 nm) packed with concentric or parallel stacked membrane lamellae ('onion', or the TAs' 'croissant-looking vacuole', on TEM; makes the cytoplasm look foamy on H&E).
Contents = surfactant (phospholipids, mainly DPPC, plus cholesterol and surfactant proteins), released by exocytosis at the apical surface.
Lamellar bodies are the hallmark of the type II pneumocyte (TA: 'be able to recognize a lamellar body').

WhyInhaled carbon is engulfed by alveolar macrophages (dust cells), which collect in septal connective tissue and travel in lymphatics to peribronchial and hilar lymph nodes, turning them black = anthracosis. Hemosiderin is golden-brown iron from red cells, not black carbon.
Key factAlveolar macrophages = dust cells: from blood monocytes; sit in the alveolar lumen and interalveolar septa; phagocytose inhaled particles (carbon, dust, pollen), microbes and erythrocytes.
Exit: the mucociliary escalator (coughed or swallowed) or lymphatics to peribronchial and hilar lymph nodes.
Anthracosis = black carbon in macrophages in the lung and hilar nodes of smokers, city dwellers and coal miners; innocuous.

What it lets you eliminate

Which statement correctly contrasts alveolar macrophages (dust cells) with type II pneumocytes?
  1. A. Type II pneumocytes cover about 95% of the alveolar surface; dust cells are attached to the capillary basement membrane
  2. B. Both are attenuated squamous cells joined by tight junctions that form the blood-air barrier
  3. C. Dust cells are monocyte-derived phagocytes in the alveolar lumen and septa that leave via the mucociliary escalator or lymphatics; type II pneumocytes are cuboidal wall cells that secrete surfactant and divide to replace type I and II cells
  4. D. Dust cells divide to replace damaged type I cells; type II pneumocytes are coughed up and swallowed after engulfing debris
  5. E. Dust cells secrete surfactant from lamellar bodies; type II pneumocytes phagocytose inhaled carbon
AnswerC. Dust cells are monocyte-derived phagocytes in the alveolar lumen and septa that leave via the mucociliary escalator or lymphatics; type II pneumocytes are cuboidal wall cells that secrete surfactant and divide to replace type I and II cells
WhyDust cells are monocyte-derived phagocytes, free in the alveoli and in the septa; loaded with carbon or hemosiderin, they leave by the mucociliary escalator or lymphatics. Type II cells stay in the wall: surfactant and stem cell. Every distractor swaps a job, a shape or a location between the cells.
Key fact
  • Type I pneumocyte: squamous, about 95% of the surface, tight junctions; gas exchange (alveolar side of the blood-air barrier); cannot divide
  • Type II pneumocyte: cuboidal cell in the wall at septal corners, apical microvilli, lamellar bodies; secretes surfactant and is the stem cell for type I and II; stays in the wall
  • Alveolar macrophage (dust cell): monocyte-derived, free in the alveolar lumen or inside the septa, dark with carbon or brown with hemosiderin; phagocytoses particles, microbes and red cells (and clears used surfactant); leaves via the mucociliary escalator (swallowed) or lymphatics to the hilar nodes
TA: 'Make sure you know these three cells and their different functions.'

Which statement about pulmonary surfactant is correct?
  1. A. Its loss increases lung compliance
  2. B. It forms a phospholipid-rich film over a thin aqueous layer that lowers surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse at expiration and easing inspiration
  3. C. It is secreted directly into the alveoli by alveolar macrophages
  4. D. It has no role in local defense against bacteria
  5. E. It raises surface tension, which holds the alveoli open
AnswerB. It forms a phospholipid-rich film over a thin aqueous layer that lowers surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse at expiration and easing inspiration
WhySurfactant is a phospholipid film over a thin aqueous layer that lowers surface tension, so alveoli don't collapse at end-expiration and inflate with less force (↑ compliance, ↓ work of breathing). Its loss decreases compliance; it comes from type II cells (macrophages only clear it), and SP-A and SP-D help defense.
Key factSurfactant (from type II pneumocytes) spreads over the whole alveolar surface as a film of phospholipids and proteins over a thin aqueous layer.
Function: DECREASES surface tension at the air–liquid interface → prevents alveolar collapse at expiration (atelectasis), lets alveoli inflate with less force → ↑ compliance, ↓ work of breathing. SP-A and SP-D also aid innate defense.
Loss (premature lung, type II injury, shallow post-operative breathing) → ↑ surface tension → atelectasis, ↓ compliance, ↑ work of breathing, hypoxia.

The 1 question you might not expect it to answer is in the dropdown at the bottom.

  • Post-operative shallow breathing with lower-lobe collapse → loss of surfactant, ↑ surface tension
  • Surfactant deficiency causes ↓ compliance (not ↑ FRC or ↓ work)
  • Free response: function of surfactant

What it lets you eliminate

  • 'Increases surface tension' is always wrong
  • 'Secreted by macrophages / type I cells / goblet cells' is always wrong
  • Deficiency never increases compliance or decreases the work of breathing

By the law of Laplace (collapsing pressure P = 2T/r), how does surfactant stabilize alveoli of different sizes during expiration?
  1. A. It enlarges alveolar radius so that collapsing pressure rises
  2. B. It thickens the alveolar fluid layer to speed diffusion
  3. C. It lowers surface tension more as an alveolus shrinks, so small alveoli do not empty into larger ones
  4. D. It acts only in large alveoli, where collapsing pressure is highest
  5. E. It raises surface tension in small alveoli so they stay inflated
AnswerC. It lowers surface tension more as an alveolus shrinks, so small alveoli do not empty into larger ones
WhyCollapsing pressure rises as radius falls (P = 2T/r), so without surfactant small alveoli would empty into larger ones at end-expiration. The film concentrates as the alveolus shrinks, so it lowers T most in small alveoli; in RDS the small alveoli collapse first.
Key factLaplace: collapsing pressure = 2 × surface tension / radius → small alveoli have the highest collapsing pressure. Surfactant lowers surface tension more as alveolar radius decreases → stops small alveoli emptying into large ones, prevents end-expiratory collapse, keeps FRC.
No surfactant (neonatal RDS) → collapse of small alveoli, ↓ compliance, ↓ PaO2, rapid breathing.

Bleomycin damages the thinnest part of the alveolar wall, where O2 crosses from air to blood. Which sequence lists that barrier from the alveolar air inward?
  1. A. Alveolar macrophage → elastic fibers → endothelium
  2. B. Ciliated epithelium → basement membrane → endothelium

  4. D. Surfactant film → type I pneumocyte cytoplasm → fused basal laminae → continuous capillary endothelium

AnswerD. Surfactant film → type I pneumocyte cytoplasm → fused basal laminae → continuous capillary endothelium

Type II cells, macrophages, fibroblasts, and two separate laminae with interstitium belong to the thick portion, not the barrier.
Key factBlood-air barrier = respiratory membrane = alveolar-capillary membrane (air → blood): thin surfactant layer → attenuated type I pneumocyte cytoplasm → fused basal laminae of the type I cell and endothelium → thin continuous (non-fenestrated) capillary endothelium; about 0.2 µm at its thinnest.
NOT in it: type II pneumocytes, macrophages, fibroblasts or interstitial connective tissue, smooth muscle, cilia. Damage (bleomycin, ARDS) → leaky barrier, edema, fibrosis.
The lecture (F0712:48) lists four elements (thin endothelium, fused basal lamina, alveolar cell, thin layer of surfactant), while the TA questions ask for three layers (type I cell, fused basal laminae, endothelium).   • Bleomycin vignette: structural site of damage → fused basal laminae

  • Fenestrated or sinusoidal capillaries, and 'two basement membranes with interstitium' (that is the thick portion)

A TEM of an alveolar septum shows a capillary containing an erythrocyte. Label A is on the thin cytoplasmic layer facing the alveolar air, B on the single dark line beneath it, and C on the thin cytoplasm lining the capillary lumen. Which identification is correct?
  1. A. A capillary endothelium, B basement membrane, C alveolar epithelium
  2. B. A type II pneumocyte, B collagen fibers, C fibroblast
  3. C. A surfactant, B type I cell, C elastic lamina
  4. D. A respiratory epithelium, B capillary epithelium, C club cell
  5. E. A alveolar (type I) epithelium, B fused basement membrane, C capillary endothelium
AnswerE. A alveolar (type I) epithelium, B fused basement membrane, C capillary endothelium
WhyRead from air to blood: the outer thin sheet is type I alveolar epithelium, the single shared line is the fused basement membrane, and the layer touching the capillary lumen is capillary endothelium. A rounded cell with lamellar bodies on the same image is type II and is not part of the barrier.
Key factOn TEM, first find the alveolus (empty air) and the capillary lumen (red cells). Across the thin side between them: type I cytoplasm (air side) → one fused basal lamina → endothelial cytoplasm (blood side).
Bulges with a nucleus are endothelial or type I nuclei; a cuboidal cell with lamellar bodies = type II; regions with fibroblasts, collagen and elastic fibers = thick portion (interstitium), not the barrier.

  2. B. A: Type II pneumocyte

  4. D. B: Type I pneumocytes
  5. E. B: Type II pneumocyte
  6. F. B: Alveolar Macrophage

WhyThe thin cell layer at A lining the capillary is the type I pneumocyte that forms the blood-air barrier; B, with lamellar bodies and microvilli, is a type II cell.
Explanation from the source
Type I Pneumocytes: Gas exchange, squamous cells with tight junctions Type II Pneumocytes: Cuboidal cells with lamellar bodies. Make Surfactant. Responsible for replenishing the alveolar pneumocytes (Stem cell ability) Alveolar Macrophages: aka Dust Cells, Monocytes of the respiratory system. (Anthracosis) Pores of Kohn: Connect adjacent alveoli to equalize air pressure. Responsible for spreading pneumonia across alveoli.

A patient with ARDS has protein-rich alveolar edema. Which statement correctly contrasts the thin and thick portions of the interalveolar septum?
  1. A. The thin portion holds the fibroblasts and elastin that give recoil; the thick portion is where gas diffuses
  2. B. The thick portion stores surfactant
  3. C. The thin portion (type I cell, fused basal lamina, endothelium) is for gas diffusion; the thick portion has interstitial fibroblasts, elastic and collagen fibers and macrophages for support and recoil
  4. D. Only the thick portion contains capillaries
  5. E. Both portions have two separate basal laminae with interstitium between them
AnswerC. The thin portion (type I cell, fused basal lamina, endothelium) is for gas diffusion; the thick portion has interstitial fibroblasts, elastic and collagen fibers and macrophages for support and recoil
WhyWhere a capillary touches the epithelium the laminae fuse (thin portion = blood-air barrier, diffusion); elsewhere an interstitium of fibroblasts, elastic and collagen fibers and macrophages separates them (thick portion: scaffold, elastic recoil, tissue fluid). Swapping the two roles is the classic trap.
Key factInteralveolar septum = the whole wall between two alveoli: capillary plexus + interstitium, covered on both faces by alveolar epithelium.
  • Thin portion = blood-air barrier: type I cell + fused basal laminae + endothelium → gas diffusion
  • Thick portion: separate basal laminae with interstitial connective tissue (fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, elastic and collagen/reticular fibers, macrophages, pericytes) → mechanical support, elastic recoil, interstitial fluid; its elastic fibers are what emphysema destroys
What it unlocks: 2 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • TA review: what the septum contains that the blood-air barrier does not → an interstitial compartment with fibroblasts, elastin and collagen
  • TA review (ARDS): the barrier is for rapid diffusion, the broader septum gives structural stability and recoil
  • TA review on barrier layers: 'two basement membranes with intervening interstitium' describes the thick portion, so it is the wrong barrier answer

What it lets you eliminate

  • 'The barrier contains the fibroblasts that make elastin' and 'the septum is the main diffusion surface' are swaps
  • Neither portion stores surfactant (type II lamellar bodies do)

Straight-recall questions it answers (2)

The blood-air barrier is specialized for rapid gas diffusion, while the broader septum (with its elastin/collagen fibers) provides structural stability and recoil

Pneumococcal infection spreads through an entire lung lobe as fluid and bacteria pass between neighboring alveoli. Which structure provides this route, and what is its normal role?
  1. A. Alveolar capillaries; normally carry blood into the alveoli
  2. B. Pores of Kohn; normally equalize air pressure and allow collateral air flow between alveoli
  3. C. Lymphatics of the alveolar walls; normally drain surfactant
  4. D. Visceral pleura; normally lubricates the lung surface
  5. E. Blood-air barrier; normally exchanges O2 and CO2
AnswerB. Pores of Kohn; normally equalize air pressure and allow collateral air flow between alveoli
WhyAlveolar pores of Kohn connect neighboring alveoli: they equalize air pressure and allow collateral air circulation if a small airway is blocked, but they also let bacteria, fibrin and inflammatory cells pass from alveolus to alveolus → lobar pneumonia. They carry air, not water, blood or impulses.
Key factPores of Kohn (alveolar pores): small openings in the interalveolar septa that connect adjacent alveoli.
Normal: equalize air pressure between alveoli; collateral ventilation (air reaches alveoli whose own airway is obstructed).
Clinical: main route for alveolus-to-alveolus spread of infection → lobar pneumonia (bacteria, fluid, fibrin, inflammatory cells).
What it unlocks: 7 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • 'What is the function of the alveolar pores' → equalize air pressure (vs exchange of water, impulses, blood entry)
  • 'Function of pores of Kohn' → collateral circulation of air if obstructed
  • Lobar pneumonia, passage of fluid and bacteria between alveoli → pores of Kohn (vs blood-air barrier, capillaries, macrophages, visceral pleura)
  • Streptococcus spreads through a lobe via → pores of Kohn (vs cadherins, tight-junction destruction, facilitated diffusion)
  • TA reviews: pores connect neighboring alveoli, equalize pressure, collateral airflow; route for lobar pneumonia

What it lets you eliminate

  • Pores of Kohn are not in the nose, trachea, bronchi or glands, and never secrete surfactant
  • They do not let blood or water into the alveoli

Emphysema

A 68-year-old long-term smoker has a barrel chest, hyperinflated lungs and progressive dyspnea. Biopsy shows a few abnormally large air spaces with thin, broken walls and no fibrosis. Which component was destroyed?
  1. A. Alveolar septa (walls) and their elastic fibers
  2. B. Submucosal mucous glands
  3. C. Bronchial smooth muscle
  4. D. Submucosal cartilage plates
  5. E. Respiratory epithelial cilia
AnswerA. Alveolar septa (walls) and their elastic fibers
WhyEmphysema = permanent enlargement of air spaces distal to the terminal bronchiole by destruction of alveolar walls (septa) without fibrosis: fewer, larger air sacs, less surface, ↓ elastic recoil → air trapping and barrel chest. Squamous metaplasia and gland hyperplasia are airway changes of smoking, and fibrosis would thicken the walls.
Key factEmphysema (a COPD): irreversible enlargement of air spaces distal to the terminal bronchiole due to destruction of alveolar walls (interalveolar septa), with no significant fibrosis → fewer, larger, floppy air sacs; ↓ elasticity/recoil, ↓ gas-exchange surface, air trapping (barrel chest, flat diaphragm, hyperinflation).
Cause: mostly smoking → elastase destroys alveolar elastin (lecture F0712:45: 'destruction of alveolar walls, decreased elasticity').
What it unlocks: 3 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Control vs emphysematous lung image: 'what is emphysema?' free response
  • Smoker with barrel chest and a biopsy of huge air spaces: diagnosis and etiology → emphysema (vs pneumonia, pulmonary hypertension, fibrosis)

What it lets you eliminate

  • Cartilage, glands, cilia and bronchial smooth muscle are airway structures, not the emphysema lesion
  • Fibrosis and inflammatory infiltrate describe other diseases, not emphysema

A smoker's emphysema mainly involves the center of each acinus and spares the alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli farther out. Which segment is destroyed in this pattern?
  1. A. Segmental bronchus
  2. B. Alveolar duct
  3. C. Alveolar sac
  4. D. Respiratory bronchiole
  5. E. Terminal bronchiole
AnswerD. Respiratory bronchiole
WhyCentriacinar (centrilobular) emphysema, the smoker's pattern, destroys the respiratory bronchioles at the center of the acinus and spares distal ducts, sacs and alveoli. Panacinar emphysema (whole acinus) is the α1-antitrypsin-deficiency pattern. The terminal bronchiole lies proximal to the acinus.
Key factAcinus = everything distal to one terminal bronchiole (respiratory bronchiole → alveolar duct → alveolar sac → alveoli).
  • Centriacinar (centrilobular): smokers, upper lobes; respiratory bronchioles destroyed, distal alveoli spared
  • Panacinar: α1-antitrypsin deficiency, lower lobes; the whole acinus is enlarged
On a numbered acinus (1 terminal bronchiole, 2 respiratory bronchiole, 3 alveolar duct, 4 alveolar sac, 5 alveolus), centriacinar = 2.

What it lets you eliminate

A heavy smoker with normal α1-antitrypsin genes develops emphysema. At the molecular level, what has happened in the lung?
  1. A. Smoke stimulated fibroblasts to overproduce elastin
  2. B. Smoke oxidants oxidized a methionine in α1-antitrypsin, lowering its activity, while recruited macrophages and neutrophils released more elastase
  3. C. Smoke increased lysyl oxidase cross-linking of collagen
  4. D. α1-antitrypsin activity increased and elastase activity decreased
  5. E. Smoke caused a point mutation that blocks α1-antitrypsin secretion from the liver
AnswerB. Smoke oxidants oxidized a methionine in α1-antitrypsin, lowering its activity, while recruited macrophages and neutrophils released more elastase
WhySmoke recruits and activates macrophages and neutrophils that release elastase, and its oxidants oxidize the reactive-site methionine of α1-antitrypsin, so AAT activity falls. Unopposed elastase then digests alveolar elastin. A secretion-blocking mutation is the genetic form, not the smoker's mechanism.
Key factProtease–antiprotease balance: elastase (from macrophages and neutrophils) digests elastin; α1-antitrypsin (AAT, a liver-made serine-protease inhibitor) blocks it.
Smoking → more macrophages and neutrophils = ↑ elastase, and oxidants oxidize AAT's methionine = ↓ AAT activity → elastin destruction → emphysema. Lecture F0712:45: 'Smoking → loss of antitrypsin → elastase from macrophages destroy elastin'.
Answer wordings: 'decreased α1-antitrypsin activity', 'increased macrophage activity', 'methionine oxidation of AAT'.
q513 is keyed 'increased macrophage activity' (matching the lecture's 'elastase from macrophages'), while the genetic-deficiency questions (q381, q382, q570) key 'neutrophil elastase'. Both cells release elastase; choose whichever source the options offer.
What it unlocks: 6 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Two brothers with the same AAT deficiency, the smoker gets emphysema earlier → smoke increases protease-mediated elastin destruction and impairs antiprotease protection
  • Smoker with barrel chest and flat diaphragms: molecular cause → decreased α1-antitrypsin activity (not trypsin, not sulfhydryl reduction)
  • Tobacco free radicals oxidize a methionine of which enzyme → α1-antitrypsin
  • 'Which is true of the mechanism' → increased macrophage activity (not lack of surfactant, ↑ antitrypsin, ↓ elastase)

What it lets you eliminate

  • 'Increased antitrypsin' or 'decreased elastase' is always backwards
  • Fibrillin, tropoelastin, lysyl oxidase, type IV collagen and vitamin C options are distractors
  • 'Lack of surfactant' is RDS, not emphysema

A 32-year-old never-smoker whose sibling also has lung disease has panacinar emphysema and a markedly reduced α1-globulin band on serum protein electrophoresis. Uncontrolled activity of which enzyme destroys this patient's alveolar walls?
  1. A. Neutrophil elastase
  2. B. Alkaline phosphatase
  3. C. Collagenase from fibroblasts
  4. D. Lysyl oxidase
  5. E. Prolyl hydroxylase
AnswerA. Neutrophil elastase
WhyA low α1-globulin band = α1-antitrypsin deficiency (misfolded AAT retained in the liver). Without its inhibitor, neutrophil elastase digests alveolar elastin → early, panacinar emphysema even without smoking. Lysyl oxidase and prolyl hydroxylase build collagen and elastin; collagenase and vitamin C are distractors.
Key factα1-antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency (inherited; young non-smoker, family history, Northern European, ↓ α1-globulin peak): misfolded AAT is retained in hepatocytes (→ cirrhosis), so too little reaches the lung (→ emphysema) → unopposed neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar elastin → early-onset panacinar emphysema.
Elastase normally turns over elastin and kills microbes; AAT keeps it in check. Imbalance = tissue destruction.
What it unlocks: 6 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

  • Non-smoker with an affected sister → deficiency of α1-antitrypsin (not vitamin C, prolyl hydroxylase, ↓ elastase)
  • Mutation preventing AAT secretion → unopposed neutrophil elastase destroying alveolar elastin
  • Free response: role of elastase; why liver and lung disease differ

What it lets you eliminate

  • Collagenase, lysyl oxidase, prolyl hydroxylase, MMP/vitamin C, alkaline phosphatase
  • Excess elastin, excess collagen or TGF-β fibrosis options (emphysema is destruction, not deposition)

Lung vessels and pleura

In a lung section, a thin-walled branch of the pulmonary artery runs alongside a respiratory bronchiole. Which structures does this artery ultimately supply?
  1. A. The walls of the segmental bronchi
  2. B. The visceral pleura only
  3. C. The capillaries of the alveoli and alveolar septa
  4. D. The cartilage plates of the intrapulmonary bronchi
  5. E. The connective tissue at the hilum
AnswerC. The capillaries of the alveoli and alveolar septa
WhyBranches of the pulmonary artery follow the airways and break up into the capillary network of the alveolar septa for gas exchange. Airway walls, hilar connective tissue and pleura are fed by bronchial (systemic) arteries, which reach the respiratory bronchioles and anastomose there with pulmonary branches.
Key factPulmonary arteries (functional, deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle): branch with the bronchial tree (a branch sits next to each bronchiole and respiratory bronchiole) → capillaries of the alveolar septa → pulmonary veins, which run separately in the interlobular septa → left atrium.
Bronchial arteries (nutritive, systemic): supply bronchi, bronchioles, connective tissue and pleura down to the respiratory bronchioles, where they anastomose with pulmonary artery branches.

  • Tumor-margin image: the artery beside the airway supplies → alveoli and alveolar septa
  • Distractors in the gas-exchange question: dual blood supply, pulmonary veins with the bronchial tree

What it lets you eliminate

  • Bronchi, hilar connective tissue and large bronchioles belong to the bronchial arteries
  • Pulmonary veins do not travel with the bronchioles

[Question 56] A lung carcinoma is resected, and the tumor margin is carefully examined in the pathology department (shown in the image). The arteriole indicated by the arrow on the image is a branch from which of the following arteries? [Question 57] The artery indicated by the dagger on the image shown in Question 56 supplies blood to which of the following structures of the respiratory system?
  1. (A) Alveoli and alveolar septa

WhyPulmonary arteries follow the airways but carry deoxygenated blood to the alveolar septal capillaries for gas exchange; airway walls get bronchial arteries.
Explanation from the source
Pulmonary arteries and their branches travel with corresponding segments of the conducting airways and bring deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to capillaries in the alveolar septa for gas exchange. Oxygenated blood leaves alveoli via pulmonary venous capillaries and returns to the left atrium of the heart via the four pulmonary veins. Tributaries of the pulmonary veins travel in the connective septa, between bronchopulmonary segments, at a distance from the pulmonary arteries and conducting airways. The other structures listed receive blood from the bronchial arteries. Keywords: Pulmonary artery, alveoli
How it follows from the main questionAn artery travelling with the airways is a pulmonary artery branch, which breaks into the septal capillaries → alveoli and alveolar septa (airway walls and hilum get bronchial arteries).
